cases.title: Cooper v. Cooper
cases.facts:
A testator made a will leaving certain property to his children. However, the will also attempted to dispose of
property that actually belonged to one of his children (the 'beneficiary') and give it to a third party. The child
was thus presented with a choice: they could either accept the benefit given to them under the will and allow
their own property to be given away, or they could keep their own property and reject the benefit under the
will.
cases.issues:
1. What is the 'Doctrine of Election' in property law?
2. Can a person accept a benefit under an instrument while simultaneously rejecting a burden or a
disposition of their own property contained in the same instrument?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The party seeking to enforce the will argued that the beneficiary cannot 'approbate and reprobate' (accept and
reject) the same document. If they want the gift, they must honor the testator's wishes regarding their own
property.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The beneficiary argued that the testator had no legal right to dispose of property he didn't own, and that they
should be allowed to keep their own property without forfeiting the inheritance.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The House of Lords ruled that the beneficiary must elect between the two options; they cannot have
both.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the foundational principle of equity known as the 'Doctrine of Election' (codified in
Section 35 of the Transfer of Property Act in India). The doctrine is based on the principle that a person who
takes a benefit under an instrument must also bear the burden attached to it. If an instrument purports to
transfer property which the transferor has no right to transfer, and at the same time gives a benefit to the real
owner of that property, such owner must elect either to confirm the transfer or to dissent from it. If they dissent,
they must relinquish the benefit given to them, which then goes back to the disappointed intended transferee.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Doctrine of Election: A person cannot accept and reject the same instrument (Approbate and
Reprobate).
2. If a beneficiary chooses to keep their own property, they must forfeit the benefit granted to them under
the instrument.
3. Equity aims to fulfill the donor's intention as a whole.

cases.title: Bellamy v. Sabine
cases.facts:
A dispute arose regarding the title to a landed estate. While the litigation was actively pending in court, one of
the parties involved in the suit sold the property to a third-party purchaser who was unaware of the ongoing
legal battle. When the court finally delivered its judgment, the question arose whether the third-party purchaser
was bound by the court's decree, even though they were not a party to the suit.
cases.issues:
1. What is the doctrine of 'Lis Pendens' (pending litigation)?
2. Does a court's judgment bind a person who purchases the property during the pendency of a suit?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The successful litigant argued that if parties were allowed to sell property during a trial, no suit could ever
reach a meaningful conclusion, as the winning party would constantly find the property in new hands.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued that they were a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the litigation, and it
would be unjust to strip them of property they bought in good faith.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Court ruled against the purchaser, holding that the property remains subject to the outcome of the
litigation.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the 'Doctrine of Lis Pendens' (codified in Section 52 of the TPA). The doctrine is not
based on the concept of 'notice' but on 'necessity'. For the administration of justice, it is essential that the
decision of a court in a suit should be binding not only on the litigant parties but also upon those who derive
title from them pendente lite (during the suit). If this were not the rule, a defendant could defeat any claim by
simply transferring the property to a friend during the trial, leading to infinite litigation. Therefore, the
purchaser takes the property subject to the 'rights' eventually determined by the court.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Lis Pendens: During the pendency of a suit regarding a specific immovable property, the property
cannot be transferred in a way that affects the rights of any other party under a future decree.
2. The doctrine ensures that the court's judgment is effective and final.
3. The purchaser during litigation is bound by the result, regardless of their good faith or lack of notice.

cases.title: Tulk v. Moxhay
cases.facts:
Tulk owned a piece of land in Leicester Square, London. He sold a portion of it (a garden) to an individual
named Elms. The sale deed contained a 'restrictive covenant' stating that Elms and his heirs must keep the land
as an open space/garden and not build any houses on it. Years later, Moxhay purchased the garden area.
Moxhay's deed did not contain the restriction, but he knew about the original covenant. Moxhay intended to
build on the land, and Tulk sued for an injunction.
cases.issues:
1. Can a 'restrictive covenant' (a negative burden) run with the land and bind subsequent purchasers
who were not parties to the original contract?
2. Does equity enforce a burden on a purchaser who has notice of a restriction?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Tulk argued that Moxhay knew about the promise to keep the land green. It would be inequitable to allow him
to buy the land at a price reflecting the restriction and then ignore the restriction to make a profit.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Moxhay argued that under common law, a contract only binds the people who signed it (privity of contract).
Since he didn't sign the original agreement with Tulk, he was not bound by the restriction.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of Tulk, granting an injunction to stop the construction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a landmark principle in property law: the 'Covenant Running with the Land' in Equity. It
held that if a person purchases property with 'notice' of a restrictive covenant, their conscience is bound by that
restriction. It would be unjust for an owner to sell land cheaply because of a restriction, only for the buyer to
sell it to someone else who ignores the restriction to gain a higher value. The Court ruled that negative/
restrictive covenants (promises not to do something) are enforceable against subsequent purchasers with
notice, ensuring that the character of the neighborhood is preserved.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Restrictive (negative) covenants run with the land in equity.
2. A purchaser with 'notice' of a restriction is bound by it, even if they didn't sign the original contract.
3. This principle is the foundation of modern urban planning and 'gated community' regulations (Section
40 of the TPA).

cases.title: Madan Mohan v. Pasupati Nath
cases.facts:
A property was sold through a registered sale deed. However, at the time of the sale, the property was already
the subject of an ongoing mortgage suit in court. The purchaser claimed they were a bona fide purchaser and
that the doctrine of Lis Pendens should not apply because the litigation was not 'collusive' or fraudulent.
They also argued they had no notice of the suit.
cases.issues:
1. Does the doctrine of Lis Pendens apply even if the purchaser has no notice of the pending suit?
2. Does Section 52 of the TPA require the litigation to be 'contentious' or merely 'pending'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The purchaser argued that without a formal notice or a registered 'lis pendens' at the sub-registrar's office, a
buyer shouldn't be penalized for a secret court case.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The opposing party argued that the law in India is strict: the moment a suit is filed, the property is 'locked' to
the outcome of that suit.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Calcutta High Court ruled that Lis Pendens applies strictly from the moment the suit is filed,
regardless of notice.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified that Section 52 of the TPA (Lis Pendens) does not depend on the equitable doctrine of
'notice'. It is a rule of public policy. The mere filing of a plaint in a court of competent jurisdiction creates a
'pendency'. Any transfer made after that moment is subordinate to the eventual decree. The Court held that the
hardship to a bona fide purchaser is secondary to the necessity of ensuring that court proceedings are not
rendered futile by the unilateral acts of a party.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Lis Pendens triggers automatically upon the filing of a suit in a competent court.
2. Notice to the purchaser is irrelevant under Section 52 of the TPA.
3. Good faith is not a defense against the application of Lis Pendens.

cases.title: Ram Coomar Coondoo v. Macqueen
cases.facts:
A lady (the real owner) allowed her husband to hold himself out to the world as the absolute owner of her
property. The property stood in his name in the public records, and he managed it as his own. The husband
eventually sold the property to a third party for value. The third party conducted a reasonable search of the
records and believed the husband was the owner. Later, the lady sued to recover the property, claiming her
husband had no right to sell it.
cases.issues:
1. What is the doctrine of 'Ostensible Ownership'?
2. Can the real owner recover property from a bona fide purchaser if they allowed someone else to act
as the owner?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The lady (real owner) argued that since she never signed the deed and was the true owner, the sale was void
under the principle of 'Nemo dat quod non habet' (no one can give what they don't have).
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued that they relied on the public records and the husband's long-standing possession. The
real owner's silence and conduct 'estopped' her from now asserting her title.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ruled in favor of the purchaser, establishing the principle
of Ostensible Ownership.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the rule of equity later codified in Section 41 of the TPA. It held that where one person
allows another to appear as the real owner of an estate, and a third party purchases that estate for value in good
faith, believing the ostensible owner to be the real owner, the real owner is 'estopped' from asserting their secret
title. If the real owner's conduct (either by express consent or implied through silence) creates a false
impression of ownership, the loss must fall on the real owner rather than the innocent purchaser who acted with
due diligence.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Ostensible Ownership (Section 41 TPA): A transfer by a person who appears to be the owner (with the
real owner's consent) is valid against the real owner.
2. The purchaser must act in good faith and take 'reasonable care' to verify the transferor's power to sell.
3. Equitable Estoppel: Real owners cannot remain silent while their property is sold to innocent third
parties.

cases.title: Gullu v. Maina
cases.facts:
A person died leaving behind a widow and a daughter. The widow, who had only a 'limited estate' in the
property under the then-prevailing Hindu law, sold the property to a third party. The daughter (the 'reversioner')
challenged the sale, arguing that the widow had no right to alienate the property beyond her lifetime. During
the trial, the daughter died, and her heirs claimed the property. The question was whether the sale by a person
with a limited interest is void or voidable.
cases.issues:
1. What is the legal effect of a transfer of property by a person with a limited interest?
2. Does Section 7 of the TPA require the transferor to have the 'authority' to dispose of the property?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs argued that the widow only owned a life interest. Her attempt to sell the absolute ownership was a
nullity because she lacked the capacity to transfer more than what she owned.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued that they had paid full value and that the sale was for 'legal necessity' (to pay off the
husband's debts), which under Hindu law allowed a widow to sell the property absolutely.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Court ruled that the sale was valid if legal necessity was proven, otherwise it was only valid for
the widow's lifetime.
cases.reasoning:
The Court analyzed Section 7 of the TPA, which defines who is competent to transfer. A person is competent if
they are either the absolute owner OR authorized to dispose of property not their own (like an executor or a
widow for legal necessity). The Court held that if the widow sold the property for a recognized 'legal necessity'
(like family maintenance or religious duties), she was 'authorized' by law to transfer the absolute title. If no
necessity existed, she could only transfer her own life interest, and the sale of the absolute title would be
voidable at the option of the heirs after her death.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Competency to Transfer (Section 7 TPA): Requires ownership or specific legal authority.
2. A transfer by a person with limited authority is valid only to the extent of that authority.
3. The concept of 'legal necessity' acts as a statutory authorization to transfer property not absolutely
owned.

cases.title: Rajeshwari v. Bhurey Lal
cases.facts:
A father executed a gift deed in favor of his daughter. The deed contained a 'condition' that the daughter could
enjoy the property but was 'forever prohibited' from selling or mortgaging the property to anyone outside the
family. If she attempted to sell it to an outsider, the gift would be cancelled. The daughter eventually sold the
property to a third party, and the father's heirs sued to recover the land based on the breach of the condition.
cases.issues:
1. Is a condition 'absolutely' restraining the alienation of property valid in law?
2. What is the effect of Section 10 of the TPA on restrictive conditions in transfers?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs argued that the condition was meant to keep the ancestral land within the family lineage and that the
daughter accepted the gift knowing this restriction.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued that the condition was void because it totally stripped the owner of the essential right to
sell their property. Once you give property, you cannot take away the power of alienation.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the daughter/purchaser, holding the condition to be void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 10 of the TPA. Section 10 states that where property is transferred subject to a
condition 'absolutely restraining' the transferee from parting with or disposing of their interest in the property,
the condition is void. The only exception is a lease. The Court held that the right to alienate (sell, gift,
mortgage) is a fundamental attribute of ownership. A condition that permanently bans selling to any outsider is
an 'absolute restraint' because it practically makes the property unsellable. While a 'partial restraint' (e.g., don't
sell for 2 years) might be valid, a total ban is repugnant to the nature of a transfer and is ignored by the law. The
daughter became the absolute owner, and the father's restriction was legally non-existent.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Absolute restraint on alienation (Section 10 TPA) is void.
2. The transferee takes the property as if the condition never existed.
3. Only partial restraints that do not significantly impair the power of alienation are valid.

cases.title: Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Lal Chand
cases.facts:
A property was sold through a registered sale deed. However, the purchaser did not pay the full price at the
time of registration. The seller allowed the purchaser to take possession of the property based on a promise to
pay the balance later. When the purchaser defaulted on the balance, the seller sued to cancel the sale deed and
recover the property, claiming that the 'transfer' was incomplete due to non-payment of consideration.
cases.issues:
1. When does the 'transfer' of ownership take place in a sale of immovable property?
2. Is the payment of the full purchase price a condition precedent for the transfer of title under Section
54 of the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The seller argued that since the price (consideration) is the essence of a sale, the failure to pay the price means
the contract is breached and no title has passed to the buyer.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued that once the sale deed is signed, witnessed, and registered, the ownership passes instantly by
operation of law, regardless of whether the money was paid.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the buyer, holding that the title had passed, but gave the seller a 'vendor's
lien' for the unpaid price.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted Section 54 of the TPA. It defines a sale as a transfer of ownership in exchange for
a price 'paid or promised'. This means that a sale can be completed even if the price is only 'promised' for the
future. The Court held that in India, the transfer of title in immovable property worth over Rs. 100 occurs upon
the registration of the deed. Once registered, the buyer becomes the owner. The non-payment of the price
does not void the sale; it only gives the seller a right to sue for the money and a 'charge' (lien) on the property
for the unpaid amount under Section 55(4)(b). The seller cannot take the land back; they can only ask the court
to sell the property to recover their debt.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Ownership in a sale passes upon registration of the deed, not upon payment of the price (Section 54
TPA).
2. Sale is an exchange for a price 'paid or promised'.
3. The seller has a 'statutory charge' (lien) over the property for any unpaid purchase money (Section
55(4)(b)).

cases.title: V .N. Sarin v. Ajit Kumar Poplai
cases.facts:
A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) owned a house. The family decided to undergo a 'partition'. Following the
partition, one specific portion of the house was allotted to V .N. Sarin. He then attempted to evict a tenant from
that portion, using a specific provision of the Rent Control Act that allows a 'landlord' who has 'acquired' a
property to evict tenants for personal use. The tenant challenged the eviction, arguing that the partition was a
'transfer of property', and under the law, a person who acquires property by transfer must wait one year before
evicting a tenant.
cases.issues:
1. Is a 'Partition' of joint family property a 'transfer of property' within the meaning of the Transfer of
Property Act?
2. Does a partition create a new title or merely refine an existing one?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The tenant argued that before partition, the property belonged to the HUF entity. After partition, it belonged to
Sarin. This change of ownership is a transfer of interest.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Sarin argued that as a member of the HUF, he already had a pre-existing interest in every inch of the house.
Partition didn't give him a new right; it only changed his 'joint' enjoyment into 'exclusive' enjoyment of a
specific part.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Sarin, holding that Partition is NOT a 'transfer of property'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental ruling on the nature of partition. It held that 'transfer of property' (Section 5)
implies the passing of a right from one living person to another who previously had no right. In a Hindu joint
family, every coparcener has an interest in the property by birth. Partition is merely the process by which 'joint'
enjoyment is transformed into 'severed' enjoyment. It is an adjustment of existing rights, not the creation of
new ones. Since no new title was 'acquired' by Sarin, but merely his old title was localized, the restrictive wait
period for 'transferred' property did not apply to him.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Partition is not a 'transfer of property' under Section 5 of the TPA.
2. Partition is an adjustment of pre-existing concurrent rights into exclusive rights.
3. Rights acquired through partition are not considered 'acquisitions by transfer' for the purposes of
restrictive statutes.

cases.title: Nayar Trading Corp v. G.S. Chawla
cases.facts:
The owner of a property entered into an 'Agreement to Sell' with Nayar Trading Corp. The company paid a
significant advance (earnest money) and was put in physical possession of the property. However, the owner
never executed the final registered sale deed. Years later, the owner tried to evict the company, claiming that as
there was no registered sale deed, the company had no legal title. The company claimed protection under the
doctrine of 'Part Performance'.
cases.issues:
1. What is the 'Doctrine of Part Performance' under Section 53A of the TPA?
2. Can a person in possession under an unregistered agreement defend their possession against the real
owner?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The company argued that they had performed their part of the contract (paid money, took possession). The
owner cannot now use the lack of registration as a tool for fraud to take the property back.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The owner argued that under Section 54, a sale is only valid by registration. An agreement to sell creates no
interest in the property. Therefore, the company was a mere trespasser whose term had expired.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the company, upholding their right to stay in possession.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 53A (Part Performance). This doctrine is a 'shield', not a 'sword'. It does not give the
company the power to claim they are the 'owners', but it does give them a powerful legal defense against
eviction by the owner. The Court held that if (1) there is a written contract, (2) the transferee has taken
possession and is willing to perform the rest of the contract, then the transferor is 'debarred' from evicting them.
The doctrine prevents an owner from taking advantage of the lack of a registered deed if they have already
handed over possession and taken money. (Note: In 2001, the law was amended to require registration of even
such agreements to claim 53A protection, but the principle of part performance remains a bedrock of property
equity).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Doctrine of Part Performance (Section 53A TPA): Protects a transferee in possession under a written
contract from eviction by the transferor.
2. Section 53A acts as a 'shield' for the defendant, not a 'sword' to claim title.
3. Prevents fraud by owners who take money and possession but refuse to register the deed.

cases.title: Musahur Sahu v. Hakim Lal
cases.facts:
A debtor owed money to multiple creditors. Realizing that he could not pay all of them and that one creditor
(Creditor A) was about to obtain a court decree to seize his property, the debtor quickly sold his only piece of
land to another creditor (Creditor B) to satisfy B's debt. Creditor A challenged the sale, arguing it was a
'fraudulent transfer' intended to defeat his claim and should be void under Section 53 of the TPA.
cases.issues:
1. Does a transfer of property to one creditor to the exclusion of others constitute a 'fraudulent transfer'
under Section 53 of the TPA?
2. What is the distinction between 'preferring' one creditor and 'defrauding' creditors?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Creditor A argued that the debtor's intent was clearly to leave him with nothing. The sale was a mala fide act to
put the property beyond the reach of the court's decree.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Creditor B argued that the debtor owed him a genuine debt. Paying one's debts is a legal act. A debtor has the
right to choose which creditor to pay first if his assets are limited.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of the debtor and Creditor B, upholding the transfer.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the scope of Section 53. A 'fraudulent transfer' is one made with the intent to 'defeat or
delay' creditors. However, the Court held that 'preferring' one creditor over another is not the same as
'defeating' creditors. If a debtor has two creditors, A and B, and he transfers property to B to pay a genuine
debt, he is not defrauding A; he is simply satisfying B. The property is gone, but it was used for a legitimate
purpose (debt repayment). For Section 53 to apply, the transfer must be a sham where the debtor secretly
retains a benefit, or it must be intended to hide the property entirely. A bona fide preference of one creditor is
not a fraudulent transfer.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Fraudulent Transfer (Section 53 TPA): A transfer made with intent to defeat or delay creditors is
voidable at their option.
2. A debtor has the right to prefer one creditor over another; such a preference is not fraudulent.
3. The intent to 'prefer' is distinct from the intent to 'defraud'.

cases.title: Seth Ganga Dhar v. Shankar Lal
cases.facts:
A mortgage deed contained a clause stating that the property could only be 'redeemed' (reclaimed by the owner
after paying the debt) after a period of 85 years. The mortgagor (owner) wanted to pay the debt early and take
his property back. The mortgagee (lender) refused, pointing to the 85-year term. The owner sued, arguing that
such a long period was a 'clog on the equity of redemption'.
cases.issues:
1. What is the 'Right of Redemption' of a mortgagor?
2. Can a contract clause effectively prevent a person from ever getting their property back (Clog on
Redemption)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued the 85-year term was unconscionable. Since he was likely to die before the term ended, it
was essentially a permanent deprivation of his property. 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued 'freedom of contract'. Both parties were adults and agreed to the 85-year term. The court
should not rewrite a commercial agreement.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the lender, but established the limits of the 'clog' doctrine.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reaffirmed the fundamental maxim: 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage'. This means the lender
can never become the owner, and the owner must always have a right to get the property back. Any clause that
makes the property 'irredeemable' is a 'clog' and is void. However, the Court held that a long period for
redemption (like 85 years) is not automatically a clog. It only becomes a clog if the terms are so harsh or
oppressive that they indicate the lender intended to grab the property. In this case, there was no evidence of
fraud or oppression; it was a simple long-term loan. Thus, the 85-year term was valid. The doctrine of 'clog' is
an equitable protection against exploitation, not a tool to bypass agreed-upon timelines.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right of Redemption (Section 60 TPA): The mortgagor has an absolute right to reclaim the property
upon paying the debt.
2. 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage': Any clause that destroys the right to redeem is void as a 'clog'.
3. A long period for redemption is not a clog unless it is accompanied by oppressive or unconscionable
terms.

cases.title: Byramjee Jeejeebhoy v. Maharashtra
cases.facts:
The State of Maharashtra enacted a law (the Ceiling Act) limiting the amount of land a person could own. Any
surplus land was to be 'vested' in the State. Byramjee Jeejeebhoy, who owned massive estates, challenged the
'vesting' process. The core dispute was: when property 'vests' in the state by operation of law, does it constitute
a 'transfer of property' that requires the payment of stamp duty and registration under the TPA?
cases.issues:
1. Does 'Vesting' of property in the State by operation of law (statute) constitute a 'transfer' under the
TPA?
2. What is the difference between an inter-vivos transfer and an involuntary statutory vesting?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The landowner argued that since ownership was moving from him to the State, it was a transfer. If it was a
transfer, the State must comply with all the formalities of the TPA and Registration Act.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The State argued that the TPA only applies to transfers 'by act of parties' (Section 5). When a law says property
'shall vest in the State', the title moves automatically by the force of the statute, not by a contract.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the State, holding that statutory vesting is NOT a transfer under
the TPA.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the limited scope of the Transfer of Property Act. Section 5 explicitly defines 'transfer of
property' as an act by which a living person conveys property to one or more other living persons. This is
known as a 'transfer by act of parties'. The TPA does not govern 'transfers by operation of law' (such as
inheritance, court orders, or statutory vesting). When a land ceiling act declares land to be state property, no
deed or registration is required because the statute itself is the title. The formalities of the TPA are inapplicable
to the sovereign exercise of legislative power.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The TPA only governs transfers 'by act of parties' (Section 5).
2. Transfers by 'operation of law' (statutory vesting, succession) are outside the scope of the TPA.
3. Statutory title does not require a registered deed to be effective.

cases.title: Bamdev Panigrahi v. Monorama Raj
cases.facts:
A person set up a touring cinema (a temporary movie theater) on a piece of land. The setup included a
projector, screen, and specialized seats, all of which were fixed to the ground using bolts and concrete
foundations. When the land was sold, a dispute arose: were the cinema equipment and seats 'immovable
property' (because they were attached to the earth) or 'movable property'?
cases.issues:
1. What is the test to distinguish between 'movable' and 'immovable' property?
2. Does 'attachment to the earth' automatically make an object immovable property under Section 3 of
the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
One party argued that since the machines and seats were bolted to a concrete floor and could not be moved
without dismantling the foundation, they were 'attached to the earth' and thus legally 'immovable'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The other party argued that the 'touring' cinema was by nature temporary. The intention was never to make the
equipment a permanent part of the land, but merely to use it for a few months and then move it.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Andhra Pradesh High Court ruled that the cinema equipment was 'movable property'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the 'Two-Fold Test' to define immovable property: (1) The Degree of Annexation (how
firmly it is attached), and (2) The Object/Intention of Annexation. While the equipment was bolted down, the
'Object' was the most important factor. The equipment was brought onto the land for a temporary purpose (a
touring cinema). The intention was to move it once the license expired. The Court held that if an object is
attached to the earth for the 'beneficial enjoyment of the object itself' (like a machine) and not for the
'permanent beneficial enjoyment of the land', it remains movable property. Since the cinema didn't improve the
land's value permanently, it was movable.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Definition of Immovable Property (Section 3 TPA): Involves things 'attached to the earth'.
2. The 'Object of Annexation' is the decisive test: Is it for the permanent improvement of the land or the
temporary use of the object?
3. Temporary fixtures, even if bolted to the ground, remain movable property if there is no intent of
permanence.

cases.title: Shanta Bai v. State of Bombay
cases.facts:
A landowner granted a person the right to enter his forest for 12 years and cut timber (teak, bamboo, firewood).
The State later nationalized the forests and prevented the person from cutting the trees, claiming the right was a
'lease of immovable property' which was not registered. The person argued that they were merely buying
'standing timber', which is movable property under the TPA and requires no registration.
cases.issues:
1. What is the legal distinction between 'Standing Timber' (movable) and a 'Tree' (immovable)?
2. Does a long-term right to cut forest produce constitute an interest in immovable property?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The petitioner argued that she was only buying wood. Wood is 'standing timber' which the TPA Section 3
explicitly excludes from the definition of immovable property.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The State argued that because the contract lasted 12 years, the trees would grow and draw nourishment from
the soil during that time. This made it a 'profit a prendre'-an interest in land-which is immovable property.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the 12-year contract was an interest in 'immovable property', requiring
registration.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the 'Nourishment Test'. 'Standing timber' (movable) refers to trees that are already fit for
cutting and are intended to be cut immediately; they are treated as wood, not trees. However, if a contract
allows trees to stay on the land for a long period (like 12 years) to continue growing and drawing sustenance
from the soil, it is no longer just a sale of 'timber'. It becomes a transfer of the right to use the land's fertility to
grow trees. This is an 'interest in immovable property'. Since the contract was for 12 years and was not
registered, it was legally invalid against the State.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Standing Timber (Movable): Trees intended for immediate cutting and use as wood.
2. Trees (Immovable): Trees intended to remain for a long period to draw nourishment from the soil.
3. Any right to enjoy the produce of land for a significant duration is an 'interest in immovable property'
requiring a registered deed.

cases.title: Marshall v. Green
cases.facts:
A seller sold several standing trees to a buyer with the verbal agreement that the buyer would cut them down 'as
soon as possible'. The buyer began cutting the trees, but the seller suddenly changed his mind and revoked the
permission, arguing that the sale of trees was a 'sale of interest in land', which under the Statute of Frauds had
to be in writing. The buyer sued for breach of contract.
cases.issues:
1. Is the sale of standing trees to be cut immediately a sale of 'goods' (movable) or 'interest in
land' (immovable)?
2. At what point does a tree transform from immovable to movable property in the eyes of the law?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The seller argued that trees are rooted in the earth. Any contract concerning them is a contract for an interest in
land, requiring formal written documentation.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued that the trees were bought purely for the wood. Since they were to be cut 'as soon as
possible', the land was merely a storage place, and the transaction was a simple sale of goods.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the buyer, holding that the trees were 'movable property'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the 'Immediate Severance' rule. If the agreement is that the trees are to be cut down
immediately or within a reasonably short timeframe, such that they derive no further 'benefit' or 'nourishment'
from the land, the trees are treated as 'chattels' (movable property). The land is considered only a temporary
resting place for the wood. Therefore, a verbal contract for 'standing timber' to be cut immediately is legally
valid and binding. This case provided the foundation for the 'Standing Timber' exception in Section 3 of the
Indian TPA.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'Intention to Sever' determines the legal character of trees.
2. Trees to be cut 'as soon as possible' are movable property.
3. Contracts for movable property do not require the formalities of immovable property transfers.

cases.title: S.N. Banerji v. Kuchwar Lime and Stone Co. Ltd.
cases.facts:
A company held a mining lease for limestone. The government attempted to cancel the lease and evict the
company. While the company was fighting the eviction in court, the government granted a 'license' to another
party to mine the same land. The original company eventually won the lawsuit and sued the government and
the new licensee for 'trespass' and damages. The government argued that since the company had been
physically out of possession, it could not sue for trespass.
cases.issues:
1. Does a lessee have the right to protect their possession against the whole world, including the
government?
2. What is the distinction between a 'Lease' and a 'License'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The company argued that a lease creates an 'interest in the property'. Even if they were temporarily ousted, their
legal right to possess remained intact, and any entry by others was a trespass.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The government argued that the company's lease had been cancelled, and the new party was only a 'licensee'
with permission to enter, which is a personal right and not a property right.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of the company, upholding their rights as lessees.
cases.reasoning:
The Court highlighted the power of a lease (Section 105 TPA). A lease is a 'transfer of a right to enjoy
property'. It creates a proprietary interest (a right in rem) that stays with the lessee. A 'license', conversely, is a
mere personal permission to do something on land that would otherwise be unlawful; it creates no interest in
the property. The Court held that the government's illegal cancellation of the lease did not extinguish the
company's interest. Because they were the rightful lessees, they had 'constructive possession', and the entry of
the new party was a trespass. The case established the superior protection afforded to a lessee compared to a
licensee.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A Lease (Section 105 TPA) creates a proprietary interest in the land.
2. A License (Section 52 Easements Act) is a mere personal right with no interest in property.
3. A lessee can maintain an action for trespass even against the owner if their lease is still legally valid.

cases.title: Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor
cases.facts:
The Associated Hotels allowed R.N. Kapoor to run a 'Barber Shop' in a specific room within the Imperial Hotel
in Delhi. They signed a document called a 'License Agreement'. Kapoor paid a monthly 'license fee'. Later,
Kapoor claimed he was actually a 'tenant' (lessee) and sought protection under the Rent Control Act to prevent
his eviction. The Hotel argued that since the document was titled a 'License' and they provided the furniture and
services, he was merely a licensee with no right to stay.
cases.issues:
1. How does a court distinguish between a 'Lease' and a 'License' when the document's title is
ambiguous?
2. Is 'Exclusive Possession' the decisive test for a lease?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The occupant (barber) argued that he had the keys to the room, operated his business there exclusively, and
paid monthly rent. This 'exclusive possession' is the hallmark of a lease.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The Hotel argued that they retained the right to enter for cleaning and repairs. The agreement was for a 'service'
within a hotel, making it a license.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that it was a 'Lease', and Kapoor was a tenant.
cases.reasoning:
The Court laid down the definitive 'Substance over Form' test. It held that the label given by the parties
('License') is not binding. The Court must look at the 'real intention' of the parties. The Court formulated four
tests: (1) Does the document create an interest in the property? (2) Does the occupant have 'exclusive
possession' (the right to exclude even the owner)? (3) If the answer is yes, it is a lease. The Court found that
although it was inside a hotel, the barber had total control over the specific room and the business. Exclusive
possession, coupled with a monthly payment, strongly indicates a lease. Thus, Kapoor was a tenant protected
by law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The 'Test of Exclusive Possession' is the primary indicator of a lease.
2. Courts look at the 'substance' and 'intent' of an agreement, not its 'title'.
3. A lease creates an interest in the property; a license is merely a personal permission.

cases.title: Gopal Sridhar Mahadev v. Shashi Bhushan
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged their property to a lender. The mortgage deed stated that the lender would have the right to
take 'all future structures and buildings' that might be built on the land as security for the loan. Later, the owner
built a house on the land and then tried to sell the house separately to a third party, arguing that the mortgage
only covered the 'land' as it existed at the time of the loan.
cases.issues:
1. Does a mortgage of land automatically cover future improvements and structures built on that land?
2. What is the scope of 'Accession' to mortgaged property under Section 70 of the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued that the house was a new, distinct asset. Since it didn't exist when the mortgage was signed,
the lender had no legal claim over it.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that under the law of 'Accession', anything permanently attached to the land becomes a part
of the land. The house was an improvement that increased the security value of the mortgage.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the lender, holding that the mortgage covered the new building.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 70 of the TPA, which deals with 'Accession to Mortgaged Property'. It states that if,
after the date of a mortgage, any accession is made to the mortgaged property, the mortgagee (lender) is entitled
to such accession as part of their security. The principle is based on the logic that a mortgage covers the
'property' as an evolving entity. When a building is constructed on mortgaged land, it becomes 'attached to the
earth' and inseparable from the land. Therefore, by operation of law, the building becomes subject to the
mortgage. The owner cannot strip the land of its improvements to defeat the lender's security.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Accession to Mortgaged Property (Section 70 TPA): Lenders are entitled to all permanent
improvements and structures added to the land after the mortgage.
2. Inseparable additions to land are legally treated as part of the land.
3. Protects the value of the lender's security against subsequent alterations by the owner.

cases.title: Ram Niwas v. Bano
cases.facts:
A tenant was living in a shop. The owner entered into an 'Agreement to Sell' the shop with the tenant. Later, the
owner ignored this agreement and sold the shop to a third party. The third party argued that they were a bona
fide purchaser for value without notice and that their registered sale deed should override the tenant's
unregistered agreement. The tenant argued that because he was physically in possession of the shop, the third
party was legally 'deemed to have notice' of his rights.
cases.issues:
1. Does 'Actual Possession' of a property by a person other than the seller constitute 'Constructive
Notice' to a purchaser?
2. What is the duty of a purchaser to inquire about the rights of persons in possession?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The purchaser argued they searched the registration records and found no other sale deed. They had no way of
knowing about a secret, private agreement between the owner and the tenant.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The tenant argued that the fact he was sitting in the shop was an 'open and visible' fact. A prudent buyer would
have asked the tenant: 'Under what right are you sitting here?' Failure to ask constitutes gross negligence.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the tenant, holding that the purchaser had constructive notice.
cases.reasoning:
The Court interpreted Section 3 of the TPA regarding 'Notice'. It held that 'Notice' is not just actual knowledge;
it includes 'Constructive Notice'. Under the law, if a person is in actual possession of a property, a purchaser is
'deemed to have notice' of all the rights which that person may have. The presence of a tenant is a 'signpost' that
should alert any reasonable buyer to investigate. If a buyer fails to inquire from the person in possession, they
are guilty of 'willful abstention from an inquiry' and cannot claim to be a bona fide purchaser without notice.
The tenant's agreement to sell was therefore binding on the third party.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Constructive Notice (Section 3 TPA): Actual possession by a third party is notice of their legal rights.
2. Duty of Inquiry: Purchasers must investigate the status of any person physically occupying the
property.
3. A purchaser who fails to inquire about a tenant's rights is not protected as a bona fide purchaser
without notice.

cases.title: Ahmed bin Allow v. Said bin Sheiban
cases.facts:
A donor made a gift of a house to the donee. However, at the time of the gift, the donor did not have physical
possession of the house, as it was being held by a third party. The donor directed the third party to hand over
the house to the donee. The question arose whether a gift of property not in the physical possession of the
donor at the time of the gift is valid under Muslim law and the principles of the Transfer of Property Act.
cases.issues:
1. Is the delivery of possession (Hiba) a mandatory requirement for a valid gift?
2. Can 'constructive possession' satisfy the requirement of delivery if the donor is not in physical
occupation?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The party challenging the gift argued that 'Hiba' requires the physical delivery of the subject matter. Since the
donor didn't have the keys or the occupancy, the gift was incomplete and void.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The donee argued that the donor did everything possible to divest himself of the property by directing the
person in possession to recognize the donee as the new owner. This constitutes constructive delivery.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the donee, upholding the validity of the gift.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the rule of delivery of possession must be interpreted reasonably. While physical delivery is
the norm, if the property is in the occupation of a tenant or a third party, a clear declaration by the donor and an
instruction to the occupant to pay rent or attorn to the donee is sufficient to complete the gift. This is known as
'constructive delivery'. The donor's intent to relinquish control and the donee's ability to exercise ownership
rights are the decisive factors.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Delivery of possession is essential for a valid gift (Hiba).
2. Possession can be 'actual' or 'constructive'.
3. Relinquishment of control by the donor and acceptance by the donee completes the transfer even
without physical handling.

cases.title: Ariff v. Jadunath Majumdar
cases.facts:
The appellant, Ariff, orally agreed to grant a permanent lease of a piece of land to the respondent, Jadunath.
Jadunath took possession and built expensive structures on the land. However, no formal registered lease deed
was ever executed. Later, Ariff sued to evict Jadunath, claiming that since the lease was not registered,
Jadunath was a mere month-to-month tenant whose term had expired. Jadunath pleaded 'equitable estoppel',
arguing that Ariff allowed him to spend money on the land.
cases.issues:
1. Can the equitable doctrine of 'part performance' or 'estoppel' override the mandatory registration
requirements of the TPA?
2. Is an oral agreement for a permanent lease enforceable against the owner?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner (Ariff) argued that under Section 107 of the TPA, a permanent lease must be registered. An oral
agreement creates no title, and equity cannot be used to bypass a specific statutory mandate.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The occupier (Jadunath) argued that it would be fraudulent to evict him after he had spent a fortune on the land
with the owner's knowledge and based on the owner's promise.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of the owner, Ariff, allowing the eviction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strict interpretation of the law. It held that where a statute (like the TPA or Registration
Act) explicitly requires a registered instrument to create a legal interest, the courts cannot use 'equitable
doctrines' to create that interest. To do so would be to effectively repeal the statute. The Court noted that in
India, unlike England, the law is codified. Therefore, Jadunath could not claim a permanent right without a
registered deed. (Note: This harsh result led to the subsequent legislative insertion of Section 53A into the
TPA to provide a limited defense of 'Part Performance' to such occupiers).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Statutory requirements for registration are mandatory and cannot be overridden by broad equitable
claims.
2. An unregistered lease deed for a term exceeding one year is inadmissible as evidence of a permanent
lease.
3. Equity follows the law; it cannot operate in direct contradiction to a specific statutory provision.

cases.title: K. Balakrishnan v. K. Kamalam
cases.facts:
A mother executed a gift deed of her property in favor of her minor son. The deed was duly registered. The
mother, acting as the natural guardian, accepted the gift on behalf of the minor. However, she retained the right
to enjoy the property during her lifetime. Years later, when the son reached majority, the mother attempted to
revoke the gift, arguing that it was never 'accepted' by the son and that she never handed over possession.
cases.issues:
1. Can a minor 'accept' a gift, and who can accept it on their behalf?
2. Does the donor's retention of a life interest (possession) in the property invalidate a gift?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The mother argued that a gift is a contract requiring acceptance. A minor is incompetent to contract and thus
cannot accept a gift. Since she never gave up possession, the gift was incomplete.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The son argued that the registered deed and the mother's own signature as guardian accepting the gift made the
transfer absolute. Possession for life was merely a restriction on enjoyment, not a denial of title.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the son, holding the gift to be valid and irrevocable.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified Section 122 of the TPA. It held that while a minor cannot contract, they can certainly be a
'transferee'. A gift can be accepted on behalf of a minor by their natural guardian. In this case, the mother
herself acted as both donor and guardian-acceptor. The registration of the deed is strong evidence of the
completion of the gift. Regarding possession, the Court held that the 'transfer of ownership' is distinct from the
'right to physical possession'. The mother transferred the 'ownership' immediately but reserved the 'possession'
for her life. This is a valid conditional gift where the son acquired a 'vested interest'.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A minor can be a valid donee, and the gift can be accepted by their guardian (Section 127 TPA).
2. Delivery of physical possession is not mandatory for a valid gift of immovable property under the TPA
if the deed is registered.
3. A donor can validly reserve a life interest in the gifted property.

cases.title: M.L. Abdul Jabbar Sahib v. M.V . Venkata Sastri
cases.facts:
A document purporting to be a mortgage was signed by the borrower and the lender. Two individuals signed the
document as witnesses. However, during the trial, it was revealed that the witnesses were not physically present
when the borrower signed the deed. They signed the document later after the borrower 'acknowledged' his
signature to them. The question was whether the document was 'attested' according to the strict definition in
Section 3 of the TPA.
cases.issues:
1. What is the legal definition of 'Attestation' under Section 3 of the TPA?
2. Can an attesting witness sign based on a 'personal acknowledgment' of the signature, or must they see
the act of signing?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The party challenging the mortgage argued that 'attested' means the witness must actually see the person sign.
Since the witnesses were in a different room, the document was not legally attested and thus invalid as a
mortgage.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that the borrower admitted the signature was his. The purpose of attestation is to ensure the
document is genuine, which was achieved by the acknowledgment.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the document was NOT validly attested, rendering the mortgage void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court gave a strict, literal interpretation to the definition of 'Attested' in Section 3. For a document to be
'attested', each witness must (1) see the executant sign, OR (2) receive from the executant a personal
acknowledgment of his signature. Crucially, each witness must sign the instrument in the presence of the
executant. The Court held that the witnesses must have the animus attestandi-the intention to bear witness
to the signature. Since the procedural sequence was not followed precisely, the document failed to meet the
statutory requirement for a mortgage, which requires attestation by at least two witnesses.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Attestation is a mandatory formality for mortgages and gifts (Section 3 TPA).
2. Personal acknowledgment is valid, but the witness must still sign in the presence of the executant.
3. Failure to comply with the strict formalities of attestation makes the document legally non-existent as a
transfer of interest.

cases.title: Siddamsetty Ajjanna v. Pangidi Satyanarayana
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his agricultural land to a lender. The mortgage was an 'Usufructuary Mortgage', where the
lender was put in possession and allowed to keep the crops as interest. The deed contained a clause stating that
if the borrower failed to repay the loan within 5 years, the mortgage would 'automatically' be treated as an
absolute sale to the lender. The borrower failed to pay, and the lender claimed ownership. The borrower sued to
redeem the property after 7 years.
cases.issues:
1. Is a 'conditional sale' clause in a mortgage deed valid?
2. Does such a clause constitute a 'Clog on the Equity of Redemption'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The borrower argued that the clause was a trap. A mortgage is a security for a loan, and the right to get the land
back (redemption) cannot be taken away by a penalty clause.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that the borrower freely agreed to the condition. It was a contract for 'Mortgage by
Conditional Sale', which is recognized by Section 58(c) of the TPA.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the borrower, allowing the redemption and striking down the clause as a
clog.
cases.reasoning:
The Court explained the difference between a 'Mortgage by Conditional Sale' and a 'Clog on Redemption'. In a
genuine mortgage by conditional sale, the transaction must be recorded in one single document as a sale with
a condition to repurchase. However, if the document is essentially a mortgage (a loan with security), the lender
cannot insert a 'forfeiture clause' that automatically converts the loan into a sale upon default. The Court held
that the 'Right of Redemption' is an inseparable attribute of a mortgage. Any agreement that shuts the door of
the court against the borrower is a 'clog' and is void in equity.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Clog on Redemption: Any provision that prevents the mortgagor from reclaiming their property after
the debt is paid is void.
2. Forfeiture clauses in mortgage deeds are illegal.
3. Section 58(c) TPA (Mortgage by Conditional Sale) requires strict adherence to its own formatting to be
valid.

cases.title: Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam
cases.facts:
A bank (the mortgagee) exercised its 'power of sale' under a mortgage deed to sell the property of a defaulter.
The bank conducted a public auction, and S.A. Kamtam was the highest bidder. The bank issued a letter of
acceptance to the bidder. However, before the formal 'Sale Deed' was registered in favor of the bidder, the
original owner (the mortgagor) rushed to the bank with the full amount of the debt and demanded his property
back. The bidder argued that the auction had already created a contract of sale, extinguishing the owner's right
to redeem.
cases.issues:
1. At what point is the 'Right of Redemption' extinguished?
2. Does a contract of sale (auction) end the mortgagor's right to reclaim the property?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued that until a formal registered sale deed is executed, he remains the owner and his statutory
right to redeem under Section 60 remains intact.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The bidder argued that once the auction is complete and the hammer falls, the owner's interest is sold. Allowing
redemption at this late stage would destroy the sanctity of public auctions.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the owner, allowing the redemption.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the intersection of Section 54 (Sale) and Section 60 (Redemption) of the TPA. In India, a
'contract for sale' does not create any interest or charge in the property; it only creates a right to obtain a deed.
The right of redemption is a statutory right that exists as long as the mortgage exists. The Court held that the
mortgage is only extinguished when the 'equity of redemption' is extinguished by the act of the parties or by a
decree of the court. The 'act of the parties' in a sale is only complete upon the registration of the sale deed.
Since the deed was not yet registered, the owner was still the owner and had the right to pay his debt and save
his property.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The Right of Redemption survives until the formal registration of the sale deed in favor of the
purchaser.
2. A mere agreement to sell or a successful auction bid does not extinguish the mortgagor's rights.
3. Section 60 of the TPA is the protector of the mortgagor's interest.

cases.title: Madam Pillai v. Badar Kali
cases.facts:
A husband orally gave a piece of land to his wife in lieu of her 'Mahr' (dower) and for her maintenance. He told
her she could enjoy the property as the absolute owner. Later, the husband's creditors tried to seize the land,
arguing that the transfer was invalid because there was no registered deed, as required by Section 54 of the TPA
for a sale or Section 123 for a gift.
cases.issues:
1. Is a transfer of property in lieu of dower (Mahr) a 'Sale' or a 'Gift'?
2. Does such a transfer require a registered instrument if the value exceeds Rs. 100?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The creditors argued that the transfer was either a sale (exchange for the debt of Mahr) or a gift. In either case,
the law requires a registered document. The oral transfer was a nullity.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that under Muslim law, a gift (Hiba) can be oral. She also argued it was a family settlement
that didn't require the formalities of the TPA.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled that the transfer was a 'Sale' and was invalid for lack of registration.
cases.reasoning:
The Court analyzed the nature of 'Mahr'. It held that Mahr is a debt. When a property is transferred to discharge
a pre-existing debt, it is an exchange of ownership for a price (the value of the debt). This falls squarely within
the definition of 'Sale' under Section 54 of the TPA. The Court held that while Muslim law allows oral gifts,
this was not a 'Hiba' (pure gift) but a 'Hiba-bil-iwaz' (gift for consideration), which is treated as a sale. Since the
value was over Rs. 100, a registered instrument was mandatory. The oral transfer conferred no title on the wife.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A transfer of property to discharge a debt (like Mahr) is legally a 'Sale'.
2. All sales of immovable property over Rs. 100 must be by a registered instrument (Section 54 TPA).
3. Religious personal laws regarding oral transfers are overridden by the mandatory provisions of the TPA
for commercial-type transactions.

cases.title: Gyanu v. Pandu
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his land. The mortgage deed contained a condition that if the borrower wanted to sell the
land in the future, he must first offer it to the lender (the mortgagee) at a fixed price that was much lower
than the market rate. The borrower later found a better buyer and challenged the condition as a 'clog' on his
right of redemption.
cases.issues:
1. Can a mortgagee insert a 'right of pre-emption' (first right to buy) into a mortgage deed?
2. Does a fixed-price buyback clause during a mortgage period constitute a clog on redemption?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The borrower argued that the clause forced him to sell his property to the lender at a loss. It effectively
prevented him from ever getting the full value of his land back, acting as a clog.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued it was a valid commercial condition. The borrower was not 'forced' to sell; but if he chose to,
the lender should have the first right.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the borrower, striking down the clause as a clog.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a mortgage is intended only as a security for a loan. A lender cannot use the borrower's
financial distress to extract a side-benefit that makes the property virtually the lender's. A clause that forces the
borrower to sell to the lender at a pre-fixed, low price is a 'clog' because it discourages the borrower from
redeeming the property. The Court reiterated that the lender must not be allowed to gain an advantage beyond
the repayment of his principal and interest. The right of pre-emption in a mortgage deed is generally viewed
with suspicion as an attempt to grab the property.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A 'right of pre-emption' at a fixed price in a mortgage deed is a clog on the equity of redemption.
2. Lenders cannot use mortgages to secure the eventual purchase of the property at an undervalue.
3. The court will strike down any collateral benefit that is unfair or oppressive to the mortgagor.

cases.title: Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash
cases.facts:
The Karta (manager) of a Hindu Joint Family (HUF) entered into an agreement to sell the ancestral property to
a third party. The Karta claimed the sale was for 'legal necessity' (to pay off debts and for family expenses). The
other family members (coparceners) filed a suit for a 'permanent injunction' to stop the Karta from selling the
property, arguing there was no real necessity.
cases.issues:
1. Can a coparcener seek an injunction to prevent the Karta from alienating joint family property?
2. What is the remedy for family members if the Karta sells property without legal necessity?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The family members argued that once the property is sold, it is difficult to get it back. To prevent 'irreparable
loss', the court should stop the sale before it happens.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The Karta and the buyer argued that the Karta has a statutory right to manage and sell property for family
benefit. An injunction would paralyze the Karta's ability to handle family emergencies.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that an injunction cannot be granted against the Karta; the remedy lies in
challenging the sale after it occurs.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that under Hindu law, the Karta has wide powers of management. If the Karta alienates
property, the other coparceners have a right to sue to 'set aside' the sale by proving there was no legal necessity.
However, the Court ruled that a suit for 'permanent injunction' is not maintainable. Granting such an injunction
would interfere with the Karta's sovereign right of management and could lead to countless frivolous lawsuits
within families. The law provides the remedy of challenging the completed transfer, which is sufficient to
protect the family's interests.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A coparcener cannot generally obtain an injunction against the Karta to stop a sale of joint family
property.
2. The Karta's power to alienate for legal necessity is a special attribute of HUF management.
3. The legal remedy is a suit to set aside the sale after the transaction is complete.

cases.title: Raju v. State of Maharashtra
cases.facts:
A person was in possession of a government land for over 30 years. When the government tried to evict him, he
claimed 'Adverse Possession', arguing that his long, continuous, and open possession had extinguished the
government's title and made him the absolute owner.
cases.issues:
1. What are the requirements to establish 'Adverse Possession'?
2. Is the limitation period for adverse possession against the Government different from that against
private individuals?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The occupant argued that his possession was 'nec vi, nec clam, nec precario' (without force, without secrecy,
and without permission). Since the government didn't evict him for three decades, they lost their right.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The State argued that mere possession, no matter how long, is not 'adverse' unless the occupant openly denies
the true owner's title. They claimed the occupant was a mere squatter.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the State, rejecting the claim of adverse possession.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified that 'possession' is not 'adverse possession'. To win a claim of adverse possession, the
occupant must prove two things: (1) Physical possession, and (2) Animus possidendi-the intention to
possess the land as an owner, in open defiance of the true owner. The occupant must show when his possession
became 'hostile'. In this case, the occupant never formally challenged the government's title until the eviction
began. Furthermore, the Court noted that under the Limitation Act, the period for adverse possession against
the Government is 30 years (compared to 12 years for private land). The burden of proof is very heavy, and the
occupant failed to show a clear, hostile, and open claim of ownership.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Adverse Possession requires proof of 'hostile' possession in open defiance of the true owner.
2. Mere long-term occupation without a claim of title is not adverse possession.
3. The limitation period against the Government is 30 years (Article 112 Limitation Act).

cases.title: T.G. Ashok Kumar v. Govindammal
cases.facts:
During a pending lawsuit for the partition of family property, one of the defendants sold a specific portion of
the land to a third-party purchaser. The purchaser bought the land in good faith and built a house. When the
partition suit was finally decided, that specific portion was allotted to a different family member, not the one
who sold it. The purchaser was ordered to be evicted. The purchaser argued that as a bona fide buyer, their
rights should be protected.
cases.issues:
1. Does the doctrine of 'Lis Pendens' cause absolute nullity of a transfer made during litigation?
2. What are the 'rights' of a bona fide purchaser pendente lite?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The successful family member argued that under Section 52, the sale was 'subordinate' to the court's decree.
Since the court gave the land to them, the purchaser has zero rights.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued they were innocent and that the seller (the other family member) had misled them. They
sought an 'equitable adjustment' to keep the land.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled against the purchaser, affirming the supremacy of Lis Pendens.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Section 52 does not make the sale 'void', but it makes it 'subordinate' to the decree. This
means the purchaser 'stands in the shoes' of the seller. If the seller loses the case, the purchaser also loses the
land. The Court emphasized that there is no 'good faith' exception to Lis Pendens. If a person buys property
involved in a lawsuit, they take a gamble on the outcome. The Court noted the hardship to the purchaser but
ruled that the integrity of the judicial process must prevail. The purchaser's only remedy was to sue the seller
for a refund of the money.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Lis Pendens (Section 52 TPA) is an absolute rule; it is not affected by the purchaser's good faith or lack
of notice.
2. A transfer during litigation is not void, but its validity is entirely dependent on the final result of the
suit.
3. Purchasers have a duty to verify if a property is under litigation before buying.

cases.title: H.V . Low & Co. Ltd. v. Jyoti Prosad Singh
cases.facts:
A person agreed to grant a mining lease to a company. The agreement stated that the owner had a 'good title' to
the land. However, when the company investigated, they found that the land was subject to certain ancestral
'maintenance charges' (rights of female relatives to receive money from the land's income). The company
refused to complete the lease, arguing the title was not 'free from doubt'. The owner sued for breach of contract.
cases.issues:
1. What is the duty of a seller/lessor to disclose defects in title under Section 55 of the TPA?
2. What constitutes a 'material defect' in a property's title?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The company argued that a 'good title' means a title that a reasonable purchaser would accept without fear of
future lawsuits. The maintenance charges were a hidden 'encumbrance' that made the title defective.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The owner argued that the charges were minor and didn't prevent the company from mining. He claimed the
company was using it as an excuse to back out of a bad deal.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of the company, holding the title was defective.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that under Section 55(1)(a) of the TPA, a seller is bound to disclose any 'material defect' in the
title of which the seller is aware and the buyer is not. A material defect is one that is so important that if the
buyer had known about it, they might not have entered the contract. The Court ruled that any hidden liability or
charge on the land (like a right to maintenance or an undisclosed mortgage) is a material defect. A buyer is
entitled to a 'marketable title' free from any reasonable doubt or hidden burden. Since the owner failed to
provide such a title, the company was justified in rejecting the lease.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Sellers must disclose all 'material defects' in title (Section 55(1)(a) TPA).
2. A material defect is one that significantly affects the value or peaceful enjoyment of the property.
3. A purchaser has the legal right to refuse to complete a transaction if the title is not 'marketable' and 'free
from doubt'.

cases.title: Shri Ram Mandir v. State of Rajasthan
cases.facts:
A piece of land was gifted to a temple 'for as long as the temple exists and continues religious services'. Years
later, the temple became dilapidated and the services stopped. The heirs of the original donor sued to recover
the land, arguing that the gift was a 'conditional transfer' and the land must return to them because the condition
was no longer being fulfilled.
cases.issues:
1. Can a gift be made subject to a 'condition subsequent' under Section 31 of the TPA?
2. What happens to a property if the condition on which the transfer depends fails?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs argued that the gift was not absolute. It was a 'determinable' interest. Once the purpose (religious
service) ended, the interest of the temple automatically ceased, and the property 'reverted' to the donor's family.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The temple management argued that once a gift is made and registered, it becomes the absolute property of the
deity. A donor cannot take back what they have given for a divine cause.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the heirs, allowing the reversion of the property.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 31 of the TPA, which allows a transfer to be made with the condition that the interest
shall 'cease to exist' in case a specified uncertain event happens (or doesn't happen). This is known as a
'Condition Subsequent'. The Court held that the donor's intent was clear: the land was for a specific purpose.
Since the purpose (running the temple) had permanently failed, the condition subsequent was triggered. Under
the law, the interest of the temple ceased, and the property legally reverted to the donor's estate. This is a valid
limitation on ownership recognized by property law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Condition Subsequent (Section 31 TPA): An interest in property can be made to end upon the
happening of a specific event.
2. If the condition of a transfer is breached, the property reverts to the transferor.
3. Determinable interests are valid in property law.

cases.title: Vikas Sales Corp v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes
cases.facts:
Under the government's import-export policy, 'Exim Scrips' (Export-Import licenses) were issued to exporters.
These scrips allowed the holder to import certain goods or could be sold in the market for a premium. A dispute
arose regarding whether the sale of these 'Exim Scrips' was a sale of 'goods' (movable property) subject to Sales
Tax, or a transfer of an 'actionable claim' (which is excluded from the definition of goods).
cases.issues:
1. What is the legal definition of an 'Actionable Claim' under Section 3 of the TPA?
2. Is a tradable license or a right to a future benefit an actionable claim or a form of intangible property?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The traders argued that an Exim Scrip is merely a right to get a license in the future. It's a 'debt' or a 'claim'
against the government. Since it's an actionable claim, it's not 'goods' and cannot be taxed.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The State argued that the scrips were bought and sold in the market like commodities. They were freely
transferable 'incorporeal' (intangible) movable property, just like a copyright or a trademark, and therefore were
'goods'.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that Exim Scrips are 'goods', not actionable claims.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the definition of 'Actionable Claim'. An actionable claim (Section 3 TPA) is a debt or a
claim to beneficial interest in movable property not in possession, which can be enforced by a lawsuit. The
Court held that an Exim Scrip is much more than a mere claim. It is a valuable right that is embodied in a
document and is ready for immediate use or market sale. It is a form of 'incorporeal movable property'. The
Court ruled that all intangible assets that are marketable-like patents, copyrights, and these licenses-are
'goods'. Therefore, they are not actionable claims and are subject to sales tax.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Actionable Claim (Section 3 TPA): A claim to an unsecured debt or a beneficial interest in property not
in possession.
2. Intangible assets that are marketable (incorporeal property) are classified as 'Goods', not actionable
claims.
3. The TPA definition of actionable claims is strictly interpreted to exclude marketable commercial rights.

cases.title: Chunilal v. Ramkishen Sahu
cases.facts:
A person owned a house and a large plot of land. He sold the house to a buyer. The only way to access the
house was through a narrow path that ran across the seller's remaining land. The sale deed did not explicitly
mention any 'right of way'. Later, the seller tried to block the path, arguing that since he didn't sell the path, the
buyer had no right to use his private land.
cases.issues:
1. What is an 'Easement of Necessity'?
2. Does a transfer of property automatically include rights essential for its enjoyment under Section 8 of
the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The buyer argued that a house without an entrance is useless. The right to use the path was an 'apparent and
continuous' easement that passed with the house by implication of law.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The seller argued that property rights are absolute. Unless a right was expressly granted in the registered deed,
it didn't exist. The buyer should have built their own road.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the buyer, upholding the right of way.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 8 of the TPA, which deals with the 'Operation of Transfer'. It states that a transfer of
property passes to the transferee all the 'legal incidents' thereof. Legal incidents include all easements annexed
to the land. Furthermore, the Court applied the doctrine of 'Easement of Necessity'. When an owner sells part of
his land and that part becomes 'landlocked', the law presumes an implied grant of a right of way over the
seller's land. Without this access, the transfer would be frustrated. Therefore, even without being written in the
deed, the right of way passed to the buyer.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Operation of Transfer (Section 8 TPA): A transfer includes all 'legal incidents' and easements necessary
for the property's enjoyment.
2. Easement of Necessity: An implied right of access is created when a property is severed from a larger
tract and becomes landlocked.
3. The law prevents a seller from rendering a sold property useless by blocking essential access.

cases.title: Gopal v. Parsotam
cases.facts:
A person died leaving two sons. The sons inherited their father's property jointly. Son A sold his 'half-share' in
the family house to a stranger (an outsider). The stranger then sued Son B for 'partition' and physical possession
of his half of the house. Son B argued that an outsider cannot be allowed to forcefully enter and live in a family
dwelling house.
cases.issues:
1. Can a co-owner of a family dwelling house transfer his share to a stranger?
2. What are the rights of a 'stranger purchaser' of a share in a family house under Section 44 of the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The stranger (purchaser) argued that as a legal owner of a 50% share, he has an absolute right to enter, live in,
and enjoy the property alongside the other brother.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The brother (Son B) argued that the house was a 'joint family dwelling house'. Allowing a stranger to move in
would destroy the family's privacy and peace. The stranger only has a right to ask for a money value or a legal
partition, not physical entry.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the brother, preventing the stranger from entering the house.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the second paragraph of Section 44 of the TPA. While a co-owner can generally transfer
their share, there is a special exception for 'dwelling houses belonging to an undivided family'. The law
recognizes the sanctity and privacy of the family home. A stranger who purchases a share in such a house does
NOT get the right to joint possession or common enjoyment of the house. The stranger's only remedy is to file
a suit for 'partition' to have a specific portion of the land separated for them. Until the house is physically
