divided by a court, the stranger must stay out. This protects families from being harassed by outsiders who buy
a share from a disgruntled relative.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A stranger purchaser of a share in a family dwelling house has no right to joint possession (Section 44
TPA).
2. The right of the stranger is limited to a 'suit for partition'.
3. Protects the privacy and 'right of residence' of undivided family members against outsiders.

cases.title: Narasimhaswami v. Venkatalingam
cases.facts:
A person executed a 'Gift' of property to a religious deity (an idol). The gift was oral, and the person handed
over possession to the temple priests. Later, the person's heirs sued to recover the land, arguing that under
Section 123 of the TPA, a gift of immovable property is only valid if made by a registered instrument. The
temple argued that a gift to a deity is a 'religious dedication' and is not governed by the TPA.
cases.issues:
1. Does the Transfer of Property Act govern gifts made to deities or for religious purposes?
2. Is a registered deed mandatory for a religious endowment of land?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs argued that the TPA is the general law of the land. Section 123 says 'for the purpose of making a
gift... the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument'. No exception is made for gods.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The temple argued that a deity is not a 'living person'. Section 5 of the TPA defines transfer as an act between
'living persons'. Therefore, the TPA doesn't apply to dedications to idols, which are governed by Hindu personal
law.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the temple, holding that the TPA does not apply to religious dedications.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental ruling on the scope of the TPA. It noted that Section 5 explicitly defines
'transfer of property' as a conveyance between living persons. An idol or a deity, while a 'juridical person'
capable of owning property, is not a 'living person' within the meaning of the Act. Therefore, the strict
formalities of the TPA (like Section 123's mandatory registration for gifts) do not apply to the dedication of
property to an idol. Such dedications are governed by the personal law of the donor. Under Hindu law, an oral
dedication accompanied by the delivery of possession is a valid and binding endowment. The deity's title was
upheld.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The TPA only governs transfers between 'living persons' (Section 5).
2. Dedications of property to deities or idols are not 'transfers' under the TPA and do not require registered
deeds.
3. Religious endowments are governed by personal laws, not the statutory formalities of the TPA.

cases.title: Kunda v. Onkar
cases.facts:
An owner of a property was being sued for a large debt. To prevent the creditor from seizing his house, the
owner executed a 'Gift Deed' in favor of his wife. The deed was registered, and he told everyone the house
belonged to her. However, in reality, the owner continued to live in the house, pay the taxes, and manage it as
his own. The creditor challenged the gift as a 'Sham Transaction'.
cases.issues:
1. What is the difference between a 'Fraudulent Transfer' (Section 53) and a 'Sham Transaction'?
2. Can a registered deed be ignored if the parties never intended for the transfer to take place?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The creditor argued that the gift was a 'Benami' or 'Sham' act. There was no 'animus transferendi' (intent to
transfer). The husband and wife conspired to create a fake paper trail to hide the assets.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that the deed was registered and the law must presume the transfer is valid. The fact that the
husband lived there was merely a marital convenience.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the creditor, declaring the gift to be a sham and void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court distinguished between two types of invalid transfers. A 'Fraudulent Transfer' under Section 53 is a
real transfer where the title actually passes to the wife, but it's done to cheat creditors. A 'Sham Transaction'
is one where the parties never intended for the title to pass; the deed is just a piece of paper meant to deceive
the world. The Court held that even if a document is registered, the court can look at the 'surrounding
circumstances' (who paid the taxes, who kept the original deed, who enjoyed the property). Since the husband's
conduct showed he never intended to give up ownership, the gift was a nullity. The house remained the
husband's property and could be seized by the creditor.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A 'Sham Transaction' is void from the beginning because there is no intent to transfer ownership.
2. Registration of a deed is not conclusive proof of a transfer if the underlying intent is missing.
3. Courts will look at the 'conduct of parties' and 'possession' to determine the reality of a property
transfer.

cases.title: Subba Rao v. Mattapalli Raju
cases.facts:
A mortgagor (borrower) failed to pay his debt. The mortgagee (lender) filed a suit and obtained a 'Preliminary
Decree' for the sale of the property. However, before the 'Final Decree' was passed and the property was
actually sold, the borrower came to court and offered to pay the full debt to get his land back. The lender
argued that once the court had passed a preliminary decree, the owner's 'Right of Redemption' was dead.
cases.issues:
1. When does the statutory Right of Redemption (Section 60 TPA) come to an end during a court
process?
2. Does a preliminary decree for sale bar the owner from paying the debt?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued that until the court actually sells the property to a third party and the sale is confirmed, he
has a legal right to save his land by paying the debt.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that the preliminary decree settled the rights of the parties. The court already ordered the
sale, so the borrower's time was up.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the borrower, allowing the redemption.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on the 'indefeasibility' of the right of redemption. It held that the right of
redemption is a statutory right under Section 60 of the TPA. This right is only extinguished by a final 'decree of
the court' or the 'act of the parties' (like a registered sale). A 'preliminary decree' is merely an intermediate step
that calculates the debt; it does not terminate the owner's title. The Court held that the owner can pay the money
and redeem the property at any time until the hammer falls in the final auction and the sale is confirmed by
the court. The law favors the owner's right to save their property over the lender's right to seize it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The Right of Redemption (Section 60 TPA) is an absolute statutory right.
2. The right survives until a 'Final Decree' is executed and the sale is judicially confirmed.
3. A preliminary decree does not extinguish the mortgagor's title.

cases.title: V . Pechi v. Perumal
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his land to a lender. The lender, while in possession of the mortgaged land, spent a large
amount of money to dig a new well and install a pump set, which significantly increased the land's value and
productivity. When the borrower came to redeem the property, the lender demanded that the borrower must pay
back the cost of the well and pump in addition to the original loan. The borrower refused, arguing he never
asked for the well.
cases.issues:
1. When can a mortgagee (lender) claim compensation for 'improvements' made to the property during
the mortgage?
2. What is the scope of Section 63A of the TPA regarding improvements?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The lender argued that the well was a 'necessary' improvement that saved the crops from drought. Since the
borrower would now benefit from a better land, he must pay the cost under equity.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The borrower argued that under Section 63A, a lender cannot force improvements on the owner to increase the
debt and make redemption more difficult (a practice known as 'improving the owner out of his estate').
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the borrower, refusing to allow the cost of the well.
cases.reasoning:
The Court interpreted Section 63A of the TPA. It held that a mortgagee is not entitled to the cost of
improvements unless the improvement was (1) necessary to prevent the property from being destroyed or
lost, OR (2) required by a public authority, OR (3) made with the express consent of the borrower. Digging a
new well for higher profits is a 'voluntary' improvement. The Court warned that allowing lenders to charge for
voluntary improvements would allow them to artificially inflate the debt so high that the borrower could never
afford to redeem the land. Since the well was not 'essential' for the property's survival, the lender bore the cost
himself, and the borrower got the well for free upon redemption.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mortgagee's Right to Improvements (Section 63A TPA): Strictly limited to 'necessary' or 'consented'
works.
2. Prevention of 'Improving the Owner Out of His Estate': Lenders cannot unilaterally increase the
redemption price through voluntary upgrades.
3. The borrower is entitled to all 'accessions' and improvements for free unless they fall under the
statutory exceptions.

cases.title: Rajeshwari v. Bhurey Lal
cases.facts:
A person executed a settlement deed in favor of his wife for her life, and after her death, to his son if the son
survived her. If the son did not survive the mother, the property was to go to the daughter. The son died during
the lifetime of his mother. When the mother subsequently died, the daughter claimed the property. The son's
widow challenged this, arguing that the son had a 'vested interest' which she should inherit.
cases.issues:
1. What is the distinction between a 'Vested Interest' (Section 19) and a 'Contingent Interest' (Section
21)?
2. Does the son's death before the life-interest holder extinguish his claim?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The son's widow argued that the moment the deed was signed, the son acquired an interest. The mother's life
estate only postponed the possession, not the ownership. Therefore, it was a vested interest that passed to his
heirs.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The daughter argued that the son's interest was dependent on an uncertain event-surviving his mother. Since
he failed to fulfill that condition, his interest never crystallized into ownership, and the property moved to her
as per the alternate contingency.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the daughter, holding the son's interest was 'Contingent'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified Section 19 and 21 of the TPA. A vested interest is created when there is no condition, or the
condition is a certainty (like the lapse of time or death of someone). A contingent interest depends on an
uncertain event. Since the son's right was specifically dependent on the condition that he must 'survive the
mother', it was a contingent interest. Because he died before the event happened, the interest lapsed and never
became part of his estate for his widow to inherit.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Vested Interest (Sec 19) is not defeated by the death of the transferee before possession.
2. Contingent Interest (Sec 21) only becomes vested upon the happening of the uncertain event.
3. Survival conditions usually render an interest contingent.

cases.title: Girjesh Dutt v. Data Din
cases.facts:
A donor made a gift of her property to her nephew's daughter (A) for life, and after A's death, to A's male
descendants absolutely. However, the deed also stated that if A had no male descendants, the property would go
to the donor's nephew (B). A died without any children. B claimed the property. The gift to 'A's male
descendants' (unborn persons) was challenged as violating the rule against perpetuity.
cases.issues:
1. What is the effect of the 'Rule Against Perpetuity' (Section 14) on transfers to unborn persons?
2. Does the failure of a prior interest under Section 13/14 invalidate the subsequent transfer (Section 16)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The legal heirs of the donor argued that the gift to unborn male descendants was void because it didn't transfer
the 'entire remaining interest' of the donor as required by Section 13. Since that was void, the subsequent gift to
the nephew was also void under Section 16.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The nephew argued that since A died without children, the contingency for his gift was met, and he should be
allowed to take the property regardless of the technicalities of the prior unborn interest.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled the gift to the nephew was void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 16 of the TPA, which states that if a transfer fails because it violates the rule against
perpetuity (Section 14) or the rules for unborn persons (Section 13), then any 'subsequent' interest intended to
take effect after the failed interest also fails. The gift to the descendants was void under Section 13. Therefore,
even though A had no children, the nephew could not take the property because his interest was legally
dependent on the failure of a void prior interest. The property reverted to the donor's heirs.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 13 TPA: Transfer to an unborn person must be of the absolute remaining interest of the
transferor.
2. Section 16 TPA: If a prior interest is void for perpetuity, the subsequent interest is also void.
3. The rule against perpetuity ensures property remains in circulation.

cases.title: Whitby v. Mitchell
cases.facts:
A marriage settlement was made where property was given to the husband and wife for life, then to their child
for life, and finally to the children of that child (the grandchildren). The grandchildren were obviously unborn
at the time of the settlement. This is the classic English rule against 'double possibilities' which influenced the
drafting of Section 13 of the Indian TPA.
cases.issues:
1. Can a life estate be created in favor of an unborn person followed by another interest in that person's
offspring?
2. What is the 'Rule against Double Possibilities'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The claimants argued that property should not be tied up for generations. Giving a life estate to an unborn
person and then trying to give another interest to their children creates 'double contingencies' that are too
remote.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The proponents argued the donor had the right to chart the course of his property as long as the ultimate vesting
was within a reasonable time.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled the gift to the grandchildren was void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that you cannot give a life estate to an unborn person and then give a subsequent interest to the
child of that unborn person. This became known as the 'Old Rule against Perpetuities'. Under Indian law
(Section 13), this is prohibited because a transfer to an unborn person must be absolute. You cannot give an
unborn person a 'life interest'; you must give them the entire remaining interest of the transferor.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A life interest cannot be created in favor of an unborn person.
2. Any interest given to an unborn person under Sec 13 must be the absolute interest.
3. This prevents the 'Whittby v. Mitchell' scenario of tying up property across multiple unborn
generations.

cases.title: Gopal Sridhar Mahadev v. Shashi Bhushan
cases.facts:
A person (A) mortgaged his property to (B). B then needed money and 'mortgaged' his rights as a mortgagee to
(C). This is known as a 'Sub-Mortgage'. A (the original owner) eventually wanted to pay off the debt. He paid
the money to B and took his property back. C (the sub-mortgagee) sued A, arguing that A should have paid him
instead, and that his sub-mortgage still attached to the land.
cases.issues:
1. What are the rights of a 'Sub-Mortgagee'?
2. Is the original mortgagor bound to pay the sub-mortgagee if they have notice of the sub-mortgage?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The sub-mortgagee (C) argued that he held a valid interest in B's mortgage debt. A was aware of the sub-
mortgage and therefore could not validly discharge the debt by paying the original lender (B).
B. Defendant / Respondent
The owner (A) argued that his contract was with B. Once he paid B, his property was free. He claimed he was
not responsible for B's private debts to C.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the sub-mortgagee (C).
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a sub-mortgage is a valid transfer of the mortgagee's interest. If the original mortgagor (A)
has 'notice' of the sub-mortgage, he is legally bound to pay the sub-mortgagee (C) to discharge the debt. If A
pays B despite having notice that B has assigned the right to C, the payment is not a valid discharge. C can still
proceed against the property. This ensures that the security for the second loan (the sub-mortgage) is not
destroyed by the collusion or negligence of the original parties.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A mortgagee can validly sub-mortgage their interest in the property.
2. If the mortgagor has notice of the sub-mortgage, they must pay the sub-mortgagee.
3. The sub-mortgagee has the right to sue for sale or foreclosure.

cases.title: T.K. Lathika v. Seth Karsandas
cases.facts:
A landlord filed a suit for the eviction of a tenant on the ground that the building was required for her own
personal use. However, the landlord had only recently purchased the property. A local law (Kerala Buildings
Lease and Rent Control Act) stipulated that a person who 'acquires' a property by transfer cannot apply for
eviction of a tenant for one year from the date of such transfer. The tenant argued the suit was premature.
cases.issues:
1. Does the word 'transfer' in rent control laws include all modes of acquisition?
2. What is the effect of Section 109 of the TPA on the rights of a transferee landlord?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The tenant argued that the landlord was a transferee. The law intended to prevent 'predatory purchases' where
people buy occupied houses just to evict old tenants immediately.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The landlord argued that under Section 109 TPA, a transferee of a landlord possesses all the rights of the
original landlord. Any restriction in a local law must be interpreted narrowly.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the tenant, dismissing the eviction suit as premature.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Section 109 of the TPA provides the general rule: the buyer of a leased property 'steps into
the shoes' of the seller. However, special local laws (like Rent Control Acts) can impose reasonable restrictions
on those rights to protect tenants. The Court held that the one-year ban on eviction after a transfer was a valid
social welfare measure. Since the landlord filed the suit within months of the purchase, the suit lacked a cause
of action at the time it was filed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 109 TPA: Transferee landlord acquires all rights/liabilities of the transferor.
2. Special Rent Control laws can override general TPA rights regarding eviction.
3. Acquisitions by sale, gift, or exchange constitute 'transfer' for the purpose of such restrictions.

cases.title: Kewal Krishan v. Rajesh Kumar
cases.facts:
A person executed a 'Sale Deed' for his property in favor of his minor nephews. The deed was registered.
However, the deed explicitly stated that the sale price had not been paid and would be paid in the future. In
reality, no money ever changed hands. Years later, the seller's heirs challenged the sale, arguing it was a 'void'
transaction because a sale requires consideration.
cases.issues:
1. Is a sale deed valid if it is registered but no consideration (price) is actually paid or intended to be
paid?
2. Can a 'gift' be disguised as a 'sale' to avoid certain legal restrictions?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs argued that under Section 54, a sale is an exchange for a price. If the price is a sham, the transaction
is not a sale. If it's not a sale, and doesn't meet the requirements of a gift (like intent), it's a nullity.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The nephews argued that the deed was registered. Section 54 says the price can be 'promised'. Therefore, the
non-payment at the time of registration doesn't invalidate the owner's transfer of title.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled the sale was void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that for a 'Sale' under Section 54, the 'price' is an essential ingredient. While the price can be
'promised' for the future, there must be a genuine intention to pay. If the facts show that no price was ever
intended to be paid and the document was just a device to move property without consideration, it is a 'void'
document. A sale deed without a real price is not a sale in the eyes of the law. Since it wasn't a valid sale, no
title passed to the nephews.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Price is an essential element of Sale under Section 54 TPA.
2. A sale deed without any intention to pay consideration is void and confers no title.
3. Registration cannot validate a transaction that is fundamentally missing a statutory requirement.

cases.title: Suraj Lamp & Industries v. State of Haryana
cases.facts:
In many parts of India, people were 'buying' and 'selling' property through a set of documents: a General Power
of Attorney (GPA), a Will, and an Agreement to Sell. This was done to avoid paying high stamp duty and
registration fees on a formal 'Sale Deed'. This 'GPA Sales' trend became the standard for real estate transactions
in Delhi and NCR. The Supreme Court took notice of the impact of this on the integrity of land records.
cases.issues:
1. Can immovable property be validly transferred through a General Power of Attorney, Will, or
Agreement to Sell?
2. What is the legal status of 'GPA Sales' in the light of Section 54 of the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The State and public interest groups argued that these documents were a fraud on the exchequer and created a
'black money' economy in real estate. They did not confer legal title under the TPA.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The industry and buyers argued that these were settled practices for decades and millions of people would lose
their homes if these transactions were declared void.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that a GPA/Will/Agreement to Sell does NOT constitute a transfer of title.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling to clean up the real estate market. It held that Section 54 of the TPA and
the Registration Act are absolute: a transfer of ownership of immovable property worth over Rs. 100 can
only be done through a registered Deed of Conveyance (Sale Deed). A Power of Attorney only creates an
agency; a Will only takes effect after death; and an Agreement to Sell only creates a right to obtain a deed.
None of these documents, individually or collectively, can substitute a Sale Deed. However, to prevent chaos,
the Court held that previous GPA transactions could still be used to claim protection under 'Part Performance'
(Section 53A) or to obtain a formal sale deed, but they did not make the person a 'legal owner'.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Property title can only be transferred via a registered Sale Deed (Section 54 TPA).
2. 'GPA Sales' are not legal transfers of ownership.
3. A General Power of Attorney is revocable and does not confer any interest in the property to the agent.

cases.title: Dahiben v. Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanushali
cases.facts:
Dahiben sold her land to Arvindbhai for Rs. 1.7 crores. The sale deed was registered, and it stated that the price
had been paid via 36 different cheques. Later, Dahiben sued to cancel the sale deed, alleging that the cheques
had bounced and she was defrauded. The buyer argued that once the deed is registered, the sale is complete and
the seller cannot ask for the land back just because the price wasn't paid.
cases.issues:
1. Does the non-payment of the purchase price give the seller a right to cancel a registered sale deed?
2. What is the remedy for a seller if the buyer's cheques bounce after registration?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The seller (Dahiben) argued that 'Sale' is a contract. If the consideration fails (cheques bounce), the contract is
voidable at her option, and the land should return to her.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued that under Section 54, title passes upon registration. Non-payment only gives the seller a
right to sue for the money, not to reclaim the land.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the buyer, holding the sale deed could not be cancelled for non-
payment.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reaffirmed the strict legal position under Section 54. A 'Sale' is a transfer of ownership in exchange
for a price 'paid or promised'. Once the deed is registered, the ownership is legally transferred to the buyer. If
the buyer fails to pay the 'promised' price (including cases where cheques bounce), the seller's remedy is to file
a suit for the recovery of the money under Section 55(4)(b) of the TPA. The seller has a 'charge' (lien) on the
property for the unpaid amount, but they cannot 'un-sell' the property. The Court also noted that Dahiben had
signed the deed admitting receipt of the cheques, and the litigation was a belated attempt to harass the buyer.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Title passes to the buyer upon registration of the sale deed, even if the price is not paid.
2. Non-payment of consideration is not a ground for cancellation of a registered sale deed.
3. The seller's remedy is a 'statutory charge' for the unpaid price (Section 55(4)(b) TPA).

cases.title: Noakes & Co. Ltd. v. Rice
cases.facts:
A public house (a bar) was mortgaged to a brewery. The mortgage deed contained a 'tie-in' clause: the owner
promised that even after the mortgage was fully paid off and redeemed, he would continue to buy all his beer
exclusively from that brewery for the next 20 years. The owner paid the debt and then challenged the clause,
wanting to buy beer from elsewhere.
cases.issues:
1. Can a mortgagee (lender) impose an obligation that continues after the mortgage is redeemed?
2. Is a 'tie-in' clause that outlives the mortgage a 'Clog on the Equity of Redemption'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued that once the loan is paid, he should have his property back in the exact same condition as
before (free and clear). A lingering obligation is a 'clog' that reduces the value of his ownership.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The brewery argued freedom of contract. The tie-in was a separate commercial agreement that the owner
voluntarily accepted as part of the deal.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The House of Lords ruled in favor of the owner, striking down the clause.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established that a mortgage is a security for a debt and nothing more. The owner has a right to get
the property back 'unfettered'. Any clause that attempts to extract a 'collateral benefit' that continues after the
mortgage is redeemed is a 'clog' because the property is not truly 'redeemed' if it remains burdened by a
restrictive contract. The Court held that when the debt is gone, all relations between mortgagor and mortgagee
as such must end. The 'tie-in' clause was void because it prevented the owner from getting his property back in
its original free state.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A 'Collateral Benefit' that survives the mortgage period is a clog on redemption.
2. Upon redemption, the property must be returned to the mortgagor free from all encumbrances created
by the mortgage.
3. 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage' implies the lender cannot attach strings to the property that last
forever.

cases.title: V .C. Thani Chettiar v. Dakshinamurthy
cases.facts:
A property was sold with a 'Condition of Repurchase'. The seller sold the land to the buyer but the deed stated
that if the seller paid back the price within 3 years, the buyer would sell the land back to him. The seller did not
pay within 3 years. Later, he tried to pay and claim the land, arguing that the transaction was actually a
'Mortgage' and he had a statutory right to redeem within 30 years.
cases.issues:
1. What is the difference between a 'Sale with a condition of repurchase' and a 'Mortgage by Conditional
Sale' (Section 58(c))?
2. Does a time limit in a sale-repurchase agreement act as a bar to the seller?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The seller argued that since the land was to return to him upon payment, the intent was to create a security for a
loan. Therefore, it was a mortgage, and the 3-year limit was an illegal 'clog'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued it was an absolute sale. The repurchase was merely a 'concession' or an 'option' granted to the
seller. Since the seller missed the deadline, the option expired, and the buyer remained the absolute owner.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the buyer, holding it was a 'Sale' and not a 'Mortgage'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'intention' of the parties is the paramount test. A mortgage requires a 'debtor-creditor'
relationship. In this case, there was no evidence that the seller was 'borrowing' money; it was a straight sale
where the buyer paid the market price. The Court also looked at the document. Under the proviso to Section
58(c) of the TPA, a transaction cannot be a mortgage by conditional sale unless the condition is embodied in
the same document as the sale. While it was in the same document here, the lack of a debt meant it was just a
sale with a repurchase option. In such sales, 'time is of the essence'. If the seller misses the date, he loses the
right.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 58(c) TPA: Condition to repurchase must be in the same document to be a mortgage.
2. A 'Sale with a condition to repurchase' is not a mortgage unless a debtor-creditor relationship exists.
3. In a repurchase option, the time limit is strict and binding, unlike the right of redemption in a mortgage.

cases.title: Knightsbridge Estates Trust Ltd v. Byrne
cases.facts:
A company (Knightsbridge Estates) mortgaged its properties to a Friendly Society for a large loan. The
mortgage deed stipulated that the loan would be repaid in 80 half-yearly installments, meaning the property
could not be redeemed for 40 years. Within a few years, interest rates fell, and the company wanted to pay off
the loan early to get a cheaper loan elsewhere. The lender refused, and the company sued, arguing that a 40-
year restriction on redemption was a 'clog'.
cases.issues:
1. Is a long period of 'postponement of redemption' (40 years) automatically a clog on the equity of
redemption?
2. Can a commercial corporation claim protection from a 'clog' in a fair business deal?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The company argued that 40 years was an unreasonable time to keep property tied up. It argued that the right to
redeem should be available as soon as they have the money.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that both parties were sophisticated commercial entities. The 40-year term allowed the
lender to have a stable long-term investment. There was no oppression or unfairness.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the lender, upholding the 40-year term.
cases.reasoning:
The Court refined the 'Clog' doctrine. It held that 'clog' is an equitable rule to prevent the exploitation of a
needy borrower by a greedy lender. However, the rule does not apply to a 'fair commercial bargain' between
two companies of equal bargaining power. A long period for repayment (postponement) is not a clog unless the
terms of the mortgage are 'oppressive or unconscionable' or if the right to redeem becomes 'illusory' (e.g., the
property will be destroyed before then). Since the company was a large entity and the interest rate was fair, the
40-year term was a valid commercial condition.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Postponement of redemption is not a clog unless it is oppressive or unconscionable.
2. The 'Clog' doctrine is meant to prevent exploitation, not to allow borrowers to escape bad commercial
bargains.
3. Courts distinguish between private individual borrowers and sophisticated commercial corporations.

cases.title: Hardei v. Bhagwan Singh
cases.facts:
A person executed a gift deed of his property. The deed was signed by the donor and the donee. However, the
donor was an illiterate woman (a 'Pardanashin' lady). Later, she sued to cancel the gift, arguing that she did not
understand the nature of the document she was signing and that it was obtained by 'undue influence'.
cases.issues:
1. What is the standard of protection afforded to a 'Pardanashin' lady (a woman who lives in seclusion)
in property transfers?
2. On whom does the burden of proof lie to show that a transfer by a Pardanashin lady was voluntary
and understood?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The lady argued that she was told the document was a 'power of attorney' to manage her lands, not a 'gift' to
give them away. She had no independent legal advice.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The donee argued that the deed was registered and that she had signed it in front of witnesses. The law must
presume the validity of a registered document.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of the lady, cancelling the gift.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established a special rule of equity for 'Pardanashin' ladies. Because of their seclusion and lack of
worldly experience, the law presumes they are vulnerable to influence. Therefore, in any transfer by a
Pardanashin lady, the burden of proof shifts heavily to the 'transferee' (the one getting the property). The
transferee must prove with 'clear and convincing' evidence that (1) the lady fully understood the nature of the
deed, (2) the deed was read and explained to her in a language she understood, and (3) she had 'independent
advice'. Since the donee could not prove these, the gift was void.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Transfers by 'Pardanashin' ladies are viewed with suspicion by the law.
2. The burden of proof is on the transferee to show the transfer was voluntary and well-understood.
3. Requirement of 'independent advice' is a mandatory safeguard for such transfers.

cases.title: Mohammad Afzal v. Gulam Kasim
cases.facts:
A Nawab (ruler) of a princely state died. The government recognized his eldest son as the successor to the
'Gaddi' (throne) and the associated state lands. However, the younger sons claimed a share in the lands, arguing
that they were 'ancestral' property. The dispute was: when the government grants lands to a specific person
along with a title or office, does that land become his absolute personal property or part of the joint family
pool?
cases.issues:
1. What is the effect of an 'official grant' of land by the sovereign on family property rights?
2. Does the principle of 'primogeniture' (eldest son takes all) apply to such grants?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The younger brothers argued that the land was historically family land. The government's recognition of the
eldest son as the Nawab was for political purposes, but the 'property' should be divided among all heirs under
personal law.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The eldest son argued that the land was inseparable from the 'office' of the Nawab. The grant was 'impartible'
(indivisible). Allowing partition would destroy the status and power of the office.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of the eldest son, holding the property was 'Impartible'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court established the doctrine of 'Impartible Estates'. It held that while the general rule of personal law is
equal partition, a property can become 'impartible' by custom or by the nature of a sovereign grant. If a grant is
made for the maintenance of a title or an office (like a Nawab or a Zamindar), the land is treated as an integral
part of that office. It passes to a single heir (usually the eldest) to ensure the continuity of the dignity. The
younger members have a right to maintenance, but no right to demand a partition of the land.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Impartible Estate: A property that, by custom or grant, is inherited by a single person and cannot be
partitioned.
2. The eldest son inherits the whole estate (Primogeniture).
3. Younger family members are entitled only to 'maintenance' from the estate's income.

cases.title: Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh
cases.facts:
Bishan Singh was a co-owner of a piece of land. Another co-owner sold his share to an outsider (a stranger).
Bishan Singh immediately filed a suit to exercise his 'Right of Pre-emption'-the right of a co-sharer to buy the
property before an outsider. However, before the court could decide, the stranger-purchaser 'resold' the land to
another co-sharer (Khazan Singh), who had an equal right to pre-emption as Bishan Singh.
cases.issues:
1. What is the 'Right of Pre-emption'?
2. Can a stranger-purchaser defeat a pre-emption suit by transferring the land to another person with an
equal right?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Bishan Singh argued that his right crystallized the moment the first sale to the stranger happened. A subsequent
sale cannot destroy his pending lawsuit.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Khazan Singh argued that the 'stranger' had been removed. Now the land was with a 'co-sharer', so there was no
more violation of the pre-emption rule. Pre-emption is a 'weak right' and can be defeated by legitimate means.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Khazan Singh, holding the pre-emption right was defeated.
cases.reasoning:
The Court described pre-emption as a 'clog on the freedom of contract' and a 'weak right'. It held that for a pre-
emption suit to succeed, the claimant must possess the superior right to buy at three stages: (1) the date of sale,
(2) the date of filing the suit, and (3) the date of the decree. If at any of these stages, the 'stranger' is replaced by
someone with an equal or better right than the claimant, the suit fails. By selling to another co-sharer, the
stranger 'purged' the defect in his title. The court will not assist a pre-emptor if the land is already back in the
hands of a member of the original group.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Right of Pre-emption: A right to be substituted in place of a stranger-purchaser.
2. It is a 'weak right' and can be defeated by the purchaser transferring the land to someone with a
superior or equal right.
3. The claimant must maintain their 'superiority' throughout the litigation.

cases.title: M. Ramakrishna Reddy v. Subba Rama Reddy
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his land and a small hut on it. During the mortgage period, the borrower (mortgagor) built
a massive house on the same land with his own money. Later, the lender (mortgagee) sued for 'foreclosure'
(taking the property permanently because the debt wasn't paid). The owner argued that even if the lender takes
the 'land', he cannot take the 'new house' because the house was not part of the original mortgage.
cases.issues:
1. Does a mortgage of land include structures built on it after the mortgage?
2. Can the borrower 'separate' his new improvements to save them from the lender?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The lender argued Section 70 of the TPA (Accession). Anything attached to the land becomes a part of the
security. The new house 'acceded' to the land and is now part of the mortgage.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The owner argued it would be a windfall for the lender. The lender only lent money against a small hut; taking
a mansion for the same debt is unjust enrichment.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the lender, following the law of accession.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the strict rule of Section 70 TPA. It held that 'property' in a mortgage is not a static object but
includes all its future natural and artificial growth. When a borrower builds on mortgaged land, he is essentially
improving the security he gave to the lender. The law of 'Accession' dictates that the new house is inseparable
from the land. Therefore, the mortgage extends to the new structure by operation of law. The borrower should
have thought of this before building on land he had pledged as security. The lender was entitled to foreclose on
both the land and the house.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 70 TPA: Mortgagee is entitled to all 'accessions' (improvements) made to the property after the
mortgage.
2. Inseparable improvements (like buildings) become part of the mortgage security.
3. The borrower cannot claim a separate title to improvements made on mortgaged land.

cases.title: V . Saraswathi v. S. Ganapathy
cases.facts:
A landlord and tenant entered into a lease agreement. The lease contained a clause stating that 'the tenant shall
not sub-let the premises'. However, the clause did not state that the landlord had a 'right to re-enter' or cancel
the lease if the tenant broke this rule. The tenant sub-let the shop to a friend. The landlord sued to evict the
tenant for breach of the condition.
cases.issues:
1. Is every breach of a lease condition a ground for eviction?
2. What is the effect of Section 111(g) of the TPA on 'Forfeiture' of a lease?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The landlord argued that a condition is a condition. The tenant broke his promise, so the lease is 'forfeited' and
he must leave.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The tenant argued that under Section 111(g), a breach of a condition only leads to forfeiture if the lease
explicitly gives the landlord the right to terminate for that specific breach. Since no such 're-entry' clause
existed, the landlord can only sue for damages, not eviction.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the tenant, dismissing the eviction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the strict requirements for 'Forfeiture' under Section 111(g). For a landlord to terminate a
lease based on a breach of a condition, two things must be proven: (1) The tenant broke an express condition,
AND (2) The lease deed contains a specific clause stating that the landlord may 're-enter' the property or that
the lease shall 'become void' upon such breach. In this case, the lease banned sub-letting but forgot to include
the penalty of termination. In property law, the court 'abhors forfeiture'. Therefore, a condition without a re-
entry clause is merely a 'covenant', and its breach does not end the lease.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Forfeiture of Lease (Section 111(g) TPA): Requires a breach of an express condition and a re-entry
clause.
2. A mere prohibition in a lease without a termination clause does not allow for eviction.
3. Statutory protections for tenants are interpreted strictly against landlords.

cases.title: J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his house to a bank to secure a loan for his business. He failed to pay. The bank issued a
notice to auction the property. The owner's brother, who also had an interest in the family business, went to the
bank and paid the entire debt out of his own pocket to stop the auction. The brother then claimed that he had
now become the 'mortgagee' (lender) and had a right to keep the house until the original owner repaid him. This
is the doctrine of 'Subrogation'.
cases.issues:
1. What is the 'Doctrine of Subrogation' under Section 92 of the TPA?
2. Can a person who pays off someone else's mortgage 'stand in the shoes' of the lender?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The brother argued that by paying the debt, he 'saved' the property. Under equity and Section 92, he should
inherit all the rights and security that the bank had against his brother.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The owner argued that the brother paid as a 'volunteer' or out of family affection. This extinguished the
mortgage. The brother can sue him for the money, but he doesn't get a 'charge' on the house.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the brother, upholding his right of subrogation.
cases.reasoning:
The Court explained Section 92 of the TPA. 'Subrogation' means substitution. If a person who has an interest in
the property (like a co-owner or a subsequent lender) pays off a prior mortgage to protect their interest, they are
'subrogated' to the rights of the mortgagee they paid off. They 'step into the shoes' of the original lender. The
Court held the brother was not a mere 'volunteer' because he had a family and business interest in the property.
By paying the bank, he became the new mortgagee. This is a powerful equitable tool to ensure that the person
who actually pays for the property's safety gets the security of the property.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Doctrine of Subrogation (Section 92 TPA): A person who redeems a mortgage is substituted with the
rights of the mortgagee.
2. Subrogation is only available to persons with a pre-existing interest in the property or a registered
agreement for subrogation.
3. 'V olunteers' who have no interest cannot claim subrogation.

cases.title: Kalyani v. Narayanan
cases.facts:
A property was owned by a joint family. One member (the father) executed a 'Sale Deed' of the entire ancestral
property in favor of a stranger. The sons sued to set aside the sale, arguing the father had no right to sell their
shares. The buyer argued that since he was in possession and the sale deed was registered, he should be allowed
to stay. He also claimed he was a 'bona fide' purchaser who didn't know about the sons' rights.
cases.issues:
1. What is the effect of a sale of joint family property by the Karta without 'legal necessity'?
2. Does a purchaser get a valid title to the entire property if the Karta exceeded his authority?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The sons argued that the father could only sell his own share (e.g., 1/3rd). His attempt to sell their 2/3rd share
was 'void' because he didn't own it and there was no family emergency to justify it.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued that the Karta is the face of the family. A buyer shouldn't have to investigate the internal
dynamics of a family before buying.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the sale was valid only to the extent of the father's own share.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the principles of Hindu law and the TPA. Under Section 7 of the TPA, a person can only
transfer what they are authorized to transfer. A Karta is authorized to sell the 'entire' family property only if
there is a 'legal necessity' (e.g., to pay taxes or for a daughter's wedding). If no necessity is proven, the Karta's
act of selling the shares of his sons is an 'excess of authority'. The Court ruled that the sale is not 'void' but
'voidable' at the option of the sons. The purchaser only gets the specific share that the father personally owned.
The sons' shares were restored to them.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A Karta can only alienate the entire joint family property for 'Legal Necessity' or 'Benefit of the Estate'.
2. Without necessity, the sale is only valid for the Karta's individual share.
3. The burden of proving 'legal necessity' lies on the purchaser.

cases.title: Mangala Prasad Tamoli v. Narvadeshwar Mishra
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his house in 1960. The deed contained a clause: 'The borrower must repay the loan within
2 years. If he fails, he shall have no right to redeem the property thereafter'. The borrower failed to pay by
1962. In 1990 (28 years later), he filed a suit to redeem the property. The lender argued the suit was barred by
the 2-year contract limit.
cases.issues:
1. Can a contract clause shorten the statutory limitation period for the right of redemption?
2. Does the right to redeem survive a 'time-bar' clause in the deed?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued that under the Limitation Act, a mortgagor has 30 years to redeem. A private contract cannot
overrule an Act of Parliament and 'clog' his right.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that the parties specifically agreed to a 2-year limit. The owner's failure to pay within that
time converted the mortgage into an absolute sale to the lender.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the owner, allowing the redemption after 28 years.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic 'Clog on Redemption' ruling. It held that the Right of Redemption is a 'statutory
right' under Section 60 of the TPA, which can only be ended by a 'decree of the court'. A clause in a deed that
says 'if you don't pay by X date, you lose the right to redeem' is the quintessential 'clog' and is void. The Court
held that the parties cannot contract themselves out of the TPA or the Limitation Act. As long as the 30-year
statutory period has not expired, the owner has a right to pay and get his property back, regardless of any
'threat' or 'limit' written in the mortgage deed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. The statutory period for redemption (30 years) cannot be shortened by a contract.
2. Any clause that purports to make a mortgage 'irredeemable' after a certain date is a void clog.
3. The Right of Redemption is an 'inalienable' attribute of a mortgage.

cases.title: M.P. Housing Board v. Krishna Kumari
cases.facts:
The Housing Board allotted a house to a person under a 'Hire-Purchase' scheme. The agreement stated that the
person would pay monthly installments for 20 years, and only after the final payment would a 'Sale Deed' be
executed. During the 15th year, the person died. Her heirs claimed they were now the 'owners'. The Board
argued that since the final payment wasn't made and no deed was registered, the Board was still the owner and
could cancel the allotment.
cases.issues:
1. In a 'Hire-Purchase' agreement, when does the ownership (title) pass to the purchaser?
2. Is a hire-purchase agreement a 'transfer of property' or a mere 'contract'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs argued that they had paid 75% of the cost and were in possession. In equity, they were the owners,
and the Board's attempt to cancel was a 'forfeiture' of their rights.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The Board argued that hire-purchase is a 'contract of hire' with an 'option to buy'. Until the last penny is paid
and a deed is registered under Section 54, no ownership exists. The person was a mere 'tenant'.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Housing Board.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the legal nature of hire-purchase. It held that such an agreement is NOT a 'transfer of
property' under the TPA. It is an 'executory contract'. Ownership remains with the seller (the Board) until the
specific condition (full payment) is met and a registered sale deed is executed. The occupant is merely a
'licensee' or a 'tenant' with a right to eventually become an owner. Since the final condition wasn't met, the heirs
had no legal 'title' to the property. The Court ruled that property law requires strict adherence to registration for
title to pass.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Ownership in a hire-purchase only passes upon full payment and registration of a sale deed.
2. Hire-purchase occupants do not possess 'proprietary rights' until the contract is completed.
3. Registration is the mandatory and only gateway to legal ownership (Section 54 TPA).

cases.title: Ammanni Ammal v. Ramaswami Naidu
cases.facts:
A person (A) sold a house to (B) through a registered sale deed. A month later, A discovered that B was actually
acting as a 'Benamidar' for C, who was A's direct rival. A then sold the same house to D, claiming the first sale
was void because it was made to an undisclosed person he would never have dealt with. D sued B for
possession.
cases.issues:
1. Is a sale valid if the purchaser is a 'Benamidar' for an undisclosed principal?
2. Does a mistake regarding the identity of the transferee invalidate a transfer of property?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The second purchaser (D) argued that identity was the essence of the contract. Since A was deceived into
selling to his enemy (via B), the first contract was void for fraud/mistake, making the second sale to D the only
valid one.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The first purchaser (B) argued that in a sale of land, identity is usually irrelevant as long as the price is paid.
Ownership passed to B upon registration, and A had no right to sell the property a second time.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the first purchaser (B).
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that in a transfer of immovable property, a mistake as to the identity of the transferee does not
make the transfer void unless it is proven that the identity was a 'material ingredient' of the transaction (like a
personal service contract). In a standard sale for cash, the seller's interest is in the money. Once the deed is
registered and money paid, the title passes to the transferee named in the deed. The fact that he was buying for
someone else is a private matter between B and C and does not allow the seller to unilaterally cancel the
registered deed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A transfer of property to a Benamidar is a valid transfer of legal title (Section 5 TPA).
2. Identity of the transferee is generally not a ground to void a sale of land.
3. Registered deeds cannot be cancelled based on secret motives or undisclosed principals.

cases.title: Bhagwat Sharma v. Gopal Sharma
cases.facts:
A landlord and tenant had an oral lease for a shop. The tenant died, and his son continued the business and paid
the rent. The landlord later tried to evict the son, arguing that a lease is a personal contract that ends with the
death of the tenant, and that the son was a mere trespasser.
cases.issues:
1. Is the interest of a tenant in a 'commercial' lease heritable by his heirs?
2. Does Section 108 of the TPA provide for the continuity of leasehold rights after the death of the
original lessee?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The landlord argued that a lease is an 'agreement' between two people. Since the original tenant was dead, there
was no privity of contract with the son.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The son argued that a lease creates an 'estate' or 'interest' in the property. Like any other property interest, it is
part of the assets of the deceased and passes to the legal heirs for the remainder of the term.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the son, holding that the tenancy was heritable.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a lease is not a mere personal license; it is a transfer of a right to enjoy property under
Section 105. This right constitutes 'property'. Unless the lease deed specifically states that it is for the 'lifetime'
of the tenant only, the leasehold interest passes to the heirs of the tenant upon his death. The son 'stepped into
the shoes' of his father and could only be evicted through the legal process for a valid reason (like non-payment
of rent).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Leasehold rights are 'heritable' property interests.
2. Death of the lessee does not terminate the lease (Section 108 TPA).
3. Heirs of a tenant enjoy the same protections as the original tenant.

cases.title: Subhash Chandra v. Ganga Prosad
cases.facts:
An elderly, wealthy man executed a 'Gift Deed' of his entire estate in favor of one of his grandsons, completely
excluding his own sons and other grandsons. After his death, the excluded heirs challenged the gift, arguing
that the grandson had 'undue influence' over the grandfather because the old man was living with him and was
dependent on him for daily care.
cases.issues:
1. Does 'mere relationship' and 'dependence' give rise to a presumption of undue influence in property
transfers?
2. On whom does the burden of proof lie under Section 122 of the TPA and Section 16 of the Contract
Act?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The sons argued that the grandfather was old and feeble. The grandson was in a position to dominate his will.
The fact that the natural heirs were excluded proves the gift was not voluntary.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The grandson argued that the grandfather was of sound mind and made the gift out of special affection for him.
There is no law that requires a person to distribute their property 'equally' among all heirs.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court upheld the gift, ruling in favor of the grandson.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified that 'undue influence' cannot be presumed merely because the parties are related or one is
old. To set aside a registered gift deed, the person challenging it must prove (1) that the donee was in a position
to dominate the will of the donor, AND (2) that the donee actually used that position to obtain an 'unfair
advantage'. The Court found that the grandfather was mentally alert and had a valid reason (affection) for the
gift. Mere exclusion of other relatives is not proof of fraud. The burden of proof remains on the person alleging
undue influence.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Undue Influence (Section 16 Contract Act) requires proof of 'domination' and 'unfair advantage'.
2. Registered gift deeds (Section 123 TPA) carry a presumption of validity.
3. Donors have the absolute right to favor one relative over others.

cases.title: Shree Narayan v. State of Bihar
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his house to a bank. The bank subsequently went into liquidation. The liquidator of the
bank sold the 'mortgage debt' and the 'security' to a third party (X) without a registered deed. X then tried to sue
the borrower to sell the house. The borrower argued that X had no legal right to sue because the transfer of the
'mortgage' required registration.
cases.issues:
1. Is the transfer of a 'Mortgagee's Interest' a transfer of immovable property?
2. Does the assignment of a mortgage debt require a registered instrument?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
X argued that he only bought a 'debt' (movable property). He merely took the place of the bank to collect the
money.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The borrower argued that a mortgage is a 'right in land'. Transferring that right is a transfer of immovable
property under the TPA, which must be registered to be valid.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the borrower, holding X had no title.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a 'mortgage' consists of two parts: the debt and the security in the land. The mortgagee's
interest is an 'interest in immovable property'. Therefore, under the TPA and Registration Act, any assignment
or transfer of a mortgagee's interest in a property worth more than Rs. 100 must be done via a registered
instrument. Since X only had a letter from the liquidator and no registered deed, he was not the legal mortgagee
and had no right to foreclose or sell the house.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A mortgagee's interest is 'immovable property'.
2. Assignment of a mortgage requires a registered deed (Section 54/107 TPA principles).
3. Without registration, the assignee cannot exercise the powers of the mortgagee.

cases.title: Rampal v. Phoolchand
cases.facts:
A property was sold through a registered deed. However, the deed contained a 'condition' that the buyer must
not sell the property to anyone for 20 years. If he violated this, the seller had the right to 'buy it back' at the
original price. The buyer sold the land after 5 years to an outsider. The original seller sued to enforce the
'repurchase' clause.
cases.issues:
1. Is a 'Partial Restraint' on alienation valid under Section 10 of the TPA?
2. Does a 20-year ban on selling constitute an 'absolute' or 'partial' restraint?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The seller argued that a 20-year limit was reasonable to prevent speculation and was a 'partial' restraint, which
is allowed by law.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer argued that being unable to sell for 20 years (a major portion of a person's life) was practically an
absolute restraint, making the property a dead asset, which Section 10 prohibits.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the buyer, holding the condition void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'degree' of the restraint is the test. While a condition 'never to sell' is clearly void, a
condition that prevents sale for a very long period like 20 years also 'substantially' takes away the power of
alienation. Such a restriction is repugnant to the nature of ownership. The Court ruled that the restriction was an
absolute restraint disguised as a partial one and was therefore void under Section 10. The buyer's sale to the
outsider was valid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Substantial restraints on the duration of alienation are void under Section 10 TPA.
2. The law favors the free 'alienability' of property.
3. Conditions that make property unmarketable for long periods are against public policy.

cases.title: Vora Abbasbhai v. Haji Gulamnabi
cases.facts:
An individual purchased a property through his lawyer (agent). The lawyer knew that the property was already
subject to an earlier 'Agreement to Sell' with another party. However, the lawyer did not inform the purchaser
about this. The purchaser claimed he was a bona fide buyer without notice. The earlier party argued that the
lawyer's knowledge was legally the purchaser's knowledge.
cases.issues:
1. Does 'Notice to an Agent' constitute 'Notice to the Principal' under Section 3 of the TPA?
2. Is the purchaser bound by facts known only to his lawyer?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The purchaser argued he was personally innocent. He hired a professional to do the job, and if the professional
failed to tell him, he shouldn't lose his property.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The earlier claimant argued Section 3 TPA (Explanation III). The law creates a fiction that whatever an agent
learns during the business of the agency is known by the master. This prevents people from staying
'intentionally ignorant' through agents.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled against the purchaser, holding he had 'Constructive Notice'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the 'Doctrine of Imputed Notice' (Section 3 TPA). An agent (like a lawyer or manager) is the
eyes and ears of the principal. Any information the agent acquires while acting for the principal is legally
'imputed' to the principal. The only exception is if the agent is acting in 'fraud' of the principal. Since the lawyer
learned of the earlier agreement during the title search for the client, the client is deemed to have known it. The
purchaser was not a bona fide buyer without notice.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Imputed Notice: Notice to an agent is notice to the principal (Section 3 TPA).
2. Knowledge acquired by a lawyer during title verification binds the client.
3. Protects prior interests from being defeated by principals acting through agents.

cases.title: N. Saminathan v. P. Thangavelu
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his land. The lender (mortgagee) stayed in possession for over 60 years. The borrower's
heirs finally sued to redeem the property. The lender argued that because 60 years had passed without any
payment or claim, he had become the absolute owner through 'Adverse Possession', and the right to redeem
was extinguished by the law of limitation.
cases.issues:
1. Can a mortgagee in possession ever claim 'Adverse Possession' against the owner?
2. Does the passage of time extinguish the 'Right of Redemption' if the debt is not paid?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The lender argued that 60 years of unchallenged possession as 'owner' had wiped out the mortgage. He relied
on the old 60-year limit for redemption under the Limitation Act 1908.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The heirs argued that under the new Limitation Act 1963, the period is 30 years, but the fundamental principle
is 'once a mortgage, always a mortgage'. The lender's possession started with permission (the mortgage) and
can never become 'adverse'.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the heirs, allowing the redemption.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the relationship between a mortgagor and mortgagee is fiduciary. The lender's possession is
'derivative' and not 'adverse'. A person who enters land as a mortgagee cannot, by his own act or the mere
passage of time, change his character into an 'adverse possessor'. He must first 'surrender' the mortgage and
then re-enter as a hostile claimant to start the clock for adverse possession. Since the lender never gave up the
mortgage, the right to redeem remained alive until the statutory period of limitation expired (which the court
found had not yet happened based on acknowledgments in records).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage' prevents a lender from claiming adverse possession.
2. A mortgagee in possession is a trustee for the mortgagor.
3. Passage of time alone does not convert permissive possession into hostile ownership.

cases.title: Chouthi Prasad v. State of Bihar
cases.facts:
A mortgagee in possession of a vacant plot of land planted a large orchard of mango trees on the land. When
the mortgagor came to redeem the property, he claimed he was the owner of the trees as well. The lender
argued the trees were his 'personal property' and he should be allowed to cut them down before leaving.
cases.issues:
1. Are trees planted by a mortgagee an 'Accession' (Section 70) or a 'Movable Property'?
2. Does the owner have to pay for the trees upon redemption?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The borrower argued that under Section 70, any accession to the property belongs to the owner upon
redemption. Since the trees are rooted in the soil, they are part of the land.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that he spent his own money and labor. Taking the trees for free was a windfall for the
borrower. He claimed the right to 'sever' the accession.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the borrower, following the rule of accession.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that trees, once planted and rooted, become 'attached to the earth' and are legally part of the
immovable property. Under Section 70 and 63 of the TPA, when a mortgage is redeemed, the mortgagor is
entitled to all accessions. The Court noted a distinction: if the accession can be 'separated' without damage (like
a removable gate), the lender can take it. But trees cannot be separated without destroying them and the soil.
Therefore, they belong to the owner of the land. However, the borrower did not have to pay for them because
they were 'voluntary' improvements not necessary for preservation (Section 63).
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Rooted trees are 'accessions' to the land under Section 70 TPA.
2. Accessions that are inseparable from the land belong to the mortgagor upon redemption.
3. Lenders are not compensated for 'voluntary' accessions unless by contract.

cases.title: Lala Govind Prasad v. Jawala Prasad
cases.facts:
A person executed a 'Simple Mortgage' of his property. Later, he 'Gented' the same property to another person.
The gift deed was registered. The mortgagee (lender) later sued to sell the property because the loan was not
paid. The donee (the person who got the gift) argued that as he was the new owner and not the borrower, his
property could not be sold for someone else's debt.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Gift' of mortgaged property extinguish the mortgage?
2. Is a transferee (donee) bound by a prior registered mortgage?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The donee argued that a gift is a voluntary transfer of 'absolute' ownership. He took the property 'free' because
the gift deed didn't mention the mortgage.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that a mortgage is a 'right in rem'. It sticks to the land regardless of who the owner is. The
donor could only gift what he had left-the equity of redemption.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the lender, allowing the sale.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that under Section 48 of the TPA (Priority), a subsequent transfer is always subject to a prior
valid transfer. A 'Simple Mortgage' creates a legal charge on the property. When the owner 'gifts' the property,
he is only transferring the 'residual interest' (the right to redeem). The donee 'stands in the shoes' of the donor.
Since the mortgage was registered, the donee had 'constructive notice' of the debt. The property remained as
security, and the lender had every right to sell it to recover the money, even if it was now in the hands of the
donee.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 48 TPA: Subsequent transfers (gift, sale) are subject to prior registered encumbrances.
2. Mortgages are 'rights in rem' that follow the property into the hands of any transferee.
3. A donee of mortgaged property only acquires the 'Equity of Redemption'.

cases.title: Tansukhrai v. Nilratan
cases.facts:
An owner of a factory leased the 'entire' factory, including the land, buildings, and all 'machinery fixed to the
floor', to a tenant for 10 years. After the lease ended, the tenant refused to return the machinery, arguing that the
machinery was 'movable property' and the rules of 'lease of immovable property' under the TPA didn't apply to
it.
cases.issues:
1. When is machinery fixed to a building considered 'immovable property'?
2. Can a single lease cover both land (immovable) and machines (movable)?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued that the machines were part of the 'factory'. They were bolted to the ground for permanent
use, making them part of the building (immovable property) under Section 3.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The tenant argued that the machines could be unscrewed and moved. They were 'tools of trade' and should be
treated as movables, governed by the Sale of Goods Act/Bailment, not the TPA.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the fixed machinery was 'immovable property'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied the 'Annexation Test'. It held that if machinery is attached to the earth for the 'permanent
beneficial enjoyment' of the building as a factory, it becomes an 'accession' to the building. The machines were
not brought there for a temporary purpose but to be an integral part of the immovable asset (the factory).
Therefore, the lease of the factory included the machines as immovable property. The tenant was bound by the
TPA rules to return the 'entire' leased premises including the machines.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Machinery bolted to the floor for the permanent purpose of a factory is 'immovable property' (Section 3
TPA).
2. A lease of an industrial unit includes all permanent fixtures as part of the immovable property.
3. Attachment for 'beneficial enjoyment of the land' is the key test for fixtures.

cases.title: B.V . D'Souza v. Antonio Fausto
cases.facts:
A person occupied a flat under an agreement titled 'Leave and License'. The agreement stated that the owner
'licensed' the occupant to use the flat for a fixed monthly fee. However, the agreement also gave the occupant
the 'keys' to the flat and stated that the owner could only enter with prior notice. The occupant later claimed he
was a 'tenant' (lessee).
cases.issues:
1. Is the grant of 'Exclusive Possession' a conclusive test for a Lease?
2. Can the parties' label of 'License' be ignored by the court?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The occupant argued that since he had the keys and could exclude the owner, he had 'exclusive possession',
which under Section 105 of the TPA is the hallmark of a lease.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The owner argued that the document explicitly said 'License'. The parties intended it to be a temporary
arrangement without creating any property interest.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled it was a 'Lease'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reiterated the 'Substance over Form' doctrine. The mere use of the word 'License' or 'Licensee' does
not prevent the agreement from being a lease. The 'real test' is the intention of the parties, which is gathered
from the surrounding circumstances and the 'rights' created. The Court held that if the document grants
'exclusive possession' to the occupant, it is a lease. The fact that the owner needed permission to enter proved
that the occupant had a 'right in the property' and not just a 'permission'. Therefore, he was a tenant protected by
rent laws.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Exclusive Possession is the decisive factor distinguishing a Lease from a License.
2. Courts look at the 'intent' and 'operational reality', not just the 'heading' of the document.
3. A lease creates an 'interest in property' (right in rem), while a license is a personal right (right in
personam).

cases.title: Gopalakrishna v. Narayan
cases.facts:
A person made a gift of his land to his wife for her life, and after her death, to his son. The wife, for religious
reasons, decided to 'renounce' her life estate and went to a monastery. The son immediately claimed the
property. The other heirs challenged this, arguing that the son must wait until the mother actually 'dies' as per
the words of the deed.
cases.issues:
1. What is the 'Doctrine of Acceleration' under Section 27 of the TPA?
2. Can a subsequent interest take effect before the stated time if the prior interest fails or is surrendered?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The son argued that the mother's interest had 'expired' by her renunciation. Since the 'prior' interest was gone,
his 'subsequent' interest should 'accelerate' and take effect immediately.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The other heirs argued that the deed was a contract. The 'event' (death) had not happened, so the son's right had
not yet vested.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the son, applying the Doctrine of Acceleration.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Section 27 of the TPA embodies the 'Doctrine of Acceleration'. It states that where a
transfer creates a prior interest and a subsequent interest, and the prior interest 'fails', the subsequent interest
takes effect. The Court interpreted 'fails' broadly to include the voluntary surrender or renunciation of the
interest. The donor's intention was to give the property to the son after the wife's enjoyment was over. Since
her enjoyment ended (by renunciation), there was no reason to keep the son waiting. The son's interest
accelerated.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Doctrine of Acceleration (Section 27 TPA): Subsequent interest takes effect upon the failure/surrender
of the prior interest.
2. 'Failure' includes renunciation, death, or illegal conditions of the prior interest.
3. Acceleration fulfills the ultimate intention of the transferor.

cases.title: H.E.H. The Nizam's Religious Endowment Trust v. CIT
cases.facts:
The Nizam of Hyderabad created a massive trust for religious purposes. The trust deed stated that the income
should be used for the 'upkeep of religious sites in Mecca and Medina' (outside India). The trust claimed tax
exemption, arguing that as a 'religious endowment', its property was held in public trust. The Revenue argued
that since the benefit was for people outside India, it was not a 'charitable trust' under Indian law.
cases.issues:
1. Can a trust for 'Religious Purposes' outside India be considered a 'Public Trust' within India?
2. What is the 'Territorial' limit of the Public Trust Doctrine in property/tax law?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The Trust argued that 'Religion' is universal. The destination of the funds doesn't change the charitable and
public nature of the property held in India.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The Revenue argued that the Public Trust Doctrine and tax exemptions are based on 'public benefit' to the
Indian society. If the money leaves the country, there is no benefit to the Indian public.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled against the Trust.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that while the trust was 'religious' in nature, it was not a 'Public Trust' for the purpose of Indian
law. Public trusts are recognized because they serve a section of the 'public in India'. The Court ruled that the
State protects and grants benefits to properties that subserve the common good of its own citizens. Since the
entire income was to be spent in a foreign country, the 'public character' of the trust was lost in the eyes of the
Indian state. The property was treated as a private settlement and taxed accordingly.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Public Trust properties must subserve the interest of the public within the jurisdiction.
2. Religious endowments for foreign purposes are not 'Public Trusts' under Indian statutes.
3. The destination of the income determines the 'charitable' status of the property.

cases.title: Ram Baran v. Ram Iqbal
cases.facts:
Two brothers partitioned their family property. The partition deed included a clause: 'If either brother ever
decides to sell his share, he must first offer it to the other brother at the market price'. Years later, one brother
sold his share to an outsider without offering it to his brother. The brother sued to cancel the sale and buy the
land himself, claiming a 'Right of Pre-emption'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Pre-emption' clause in a partition deed violate the 'Rule against Perpetuity' (Section 14)?
2. Does a contract for pre-emption create an 'interest in property'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The outsider (purchaser) argued that the clause was void. It bound not just the brothers, but their 'heirs' forever.
A promise that lasts for generations violates Section 14, which requires all interests to vest within a lifetime.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The brother argued that pre-emption is a 'contractual' right. Section 14 only applies to the 'vesting of
ownership', not to a simple promise to offer land to a relative.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the brother, upholding the clause.
cases.reasoning:
The Court made a vital distinction. Section 14 of the TPA (Perpetuity) applies to 'transfers' that create an
interest in the property. The Court held that in India (under Section 54), a contract for sale (including pre-
emption) does NOT create any interest in the property; it only creates a personal obligation. Since no 'interest'
was created, the Rule against Perpetuity was not applicable. The clause was a valid contractual covenant that
was binding on the brothers and their heirs. The sale to the outsider was subject to this right.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Contracts for Pre-emption do not create an 'interest in property' (Section 54 TPA).
2. The Rule against Perpetuity (Section 14 TPA) does not apply to personal contractual covenants.
3. Pre-emption clauses in partition deeds are generally valid and enforceable.

cases.title: Chanda v. Ratna
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his land and died. He left two heirs: Heir A and Heir B. Heir A went to the lender and paid
the entire mortgage debt. Heir A then claimed that he had now become the 'mortgagee' for Heir B's share.
When Heir B tried to take his half of the land, Heir A refused, saying 'I have been subrogated to the lender's
rights'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Co-mortgagor' have a right of subrogation?
2. Can one heir become the 'creditor' of another heir by paying off a family mortgage?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
Heir A argued that under Section 92 of the TPA, a co-mortgagor who redeems the whole mortgage is
