'subrogated' to the position of the mortgagee. He now held a 'charge' on B's share for B's portion of the debt.
B. Defendant / Respondent
Heir B argued that A only paid as a family member to save the land. He should just sue B for the money, but he
cannot 'keep' the land as a lender.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Heir A.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'Doctrine of Subrogation' (Section 92) is a rule of equity and justice. If there are
multiple owners of a mortgaged property, and one of them pays the whole debt, he 'saves' the shares of others.
It is only fair that he should inherit the 'security' that the lender had. By paying the bank, Heir A 'stepped into
the shoes' of the bank. Heir B could only get his half of the land back by paying his share of the debt to Heir A.
This prevents Heir B from getting a 'free ride' at Heir A's expense.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Co-mortgagors have a statutory right of subrogation (Section 92 TPA).
2. A person redeeming a whole mortgage acquires the rights and securities of the mortgagee against other
co-owners.
3. Subrogation ensures 'contribution' among co-debtors.

cases.title: Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand
cases.facts:
A landlord filed an application before a government official (the 'Rent Control Officer') seeking permission to
evict a tenant. The law required the officer to 'be satisfied' that the landlord's need was genuine. The officer
granted the permission without holding any hearing or allowing the tenant to see the landlord's evidence. The
tenant challenged the order as a violation of natural justice.
cases.issues:
1. Is an administrative official acting under a property/rent statute bound by the 'Principles of Natural
Justice'?
2. Does an order affecting 'leasehold rights' involve a quasi-judicial function?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The tenant argued that his 'right to stay' was a property right under the TPA. Any order that evicts him has
severe 'civil consequences'. Therefore, a fair hearing is mandatory.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The landlord and the State argued that the officer was performing an 'administrative' act. The statute gave the
officer 'discretion' and did not explicitly mention a hearing.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the tenant, quashing the order.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a foundational judgment on 'Quasi-Judicial' functions. It held that even if a statute is silent
about a hearing, if the authority has the power to decide a dispute that affects the 'rights of parties' (like a lease),
the authority must act 'judicially'. Evicting a person from their home or shop is a grave matter. Therefore, the
Principles of Natural Justice-especially audi alteram partem (hear the other side)-are implied in the law.
The officer was bound to share the evidence and hear the tenant before passing the order.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Orders affecting property or leasehold rights are 'quasi-judicial' in nature.
2. Principles of Natural Justice must be followed even if the statute is silent.
3. Any administrative act with 'civil consequences' requires a fair hearing.

cases.title: Narayana v. Krishna
cases.facts:
A person executed a gift deed. He gave his property to his daughter for her life, and after her death, to 'all the
children that may be born to her'. At the time of the gift, the daughter had no children. Later, a son was born.
After the daughter's death, the son claimed the property. The other relatives challenged the gift, arguing that a
gift to an unborn person is void under Hindu law and the TPA.
cases.issues:
1. What is the procedure for making a valid gift to an 'Unborn Person' under Section 13 of the TPA?
2. Does the gift fail if the unborn person is not in existence at the time of the transfer?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The son argued that while he wasn't born when the deed was signed, he was born during the 'lifetime' of the
mother (the prior interest holder). Therefore, the gift 'vested' in him the moment he was born.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The relatives argued that a gift requires immediate 'acceptance'. Since the son wasn't there to accept, the
transfer was a nullity.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the son, upholding the gift.
cases.reasoning:
The Court explained the mechanism of Section 13. You cannot transfer property directly to an unborn
person. But you can transfer it to a living person (the daughter) for their life, and then to the unborn person. The
Court held that the unborn person must come into existence before the prior interest (the life estate) expires.
Since the son was born while the mother was still alive, the condition of Section 13 was met. The son acquired
a 'vested interest' upon his birth, and absolute ownership upon his mother's death.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 13 TPA: Gift to an unborn person requires a prior life estate in a living person.
2. The unborn person must be born before the prior interest terminates.
3. The interest given to the unborn person must be 'absolute' (the whole remaining interest).

cases.title: R.V . Bhupal v. Mallikarjuna Rao
cases.facts:
A landlord filed a suit to evict a tenant. During the suit, the landlord accepted a 'revised rent' from the tenant
and signed a new receipt. The tenant later argued that by accepting the new rent, the landlord had 'waived' his
right to evict and that a 'new lease' had been created by conduct. This is the doctrine of 'Waiver of Notice'.
cases.issues:
1. Does the acceptance of rent after the expiry of a lease constitute a 'Waiver' under Section 113 of the
TPA?
2. What is the difference between 'Waiver' and 'Holding Over'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The tenant argued that the landlord's conduct of taking money showed he intended to continue the relationship.
The previous 'Notice to Quit' was therefore cancelled by the act of the parties.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The landlord argued that he only took the money as 'compensation' for the tenant's illegal stay (mesne profits),
and that he never intended to drop the eviction suit.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the landlord, holding there was no waiver.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified Section 113. 'Waiver' of a notice to quit requires two things: (1) The act of the landlord (like
accepting rent), AND (2) The 'intent' of both parties to continue the lease. The Court held that mere acceptance
of money is not conclusive proof of waiver. If the landlord is already fighting a case in court to evict the tenant,
it shows a clear intent not to waive the notice. The money was treated as 'damages for use and occupation'
rather than rent. The Court ruled that 'intent' must be gathered from the totality of the conduct, and a pending
lawsuit is the strongest evidence against waiver.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Waiver (Section 113 TPA): Requires an express or implied intent to treat the lease as subsisting.
2. Acceptance of rent during a pending eviction suit does not automatically constitute waiver.
3. The burden is on the tenant to prove the landlord intended to start a fresh lease.

cases.title: Ramrao v. Laxman
cases.facts:
A donor made a gift to a school, with the condition: 'The school shall have the property, but if the school ever
stops teaching Sanskrit, the property shall return to me'. The school functioned for 40 years but then stopped
the Sanskrit department. The donor's son sued to recover the land. The school argued the condition was void for
'Perpetuity'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Condition Subsequent' (reversion) violate the Rule against Perpetuity?
2. What is the time limit for a condition to return property to the donor?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The donor's son argued that this was a 'Determinable Interest' under Section 31. The school only owned the
land as long as they followed the rule. Once they stopped, their title died.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The school argued that a condition that lasts 'forever' prevents the land from being truly owned or sold. Since
the 'event' (stopping Sanskrit) might happen 100 years later, the condition is void for perpetuity under Section
14.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the school, holding the condition void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a complex ruling on Section 14. It held that the 'Rule against Perpetuity' applies to any
future interest that 'vests' in a person. A right of 'reverter' (the land coming back to the donor) is a future
interest. Under Section 14, a future interest must vest within 'a life in being plus 18 years'. Since the condition
'stop teaching Sanskrit' could happen 200 years later, the interest of the donor's heirs would vest too late.
Therefore, the condition was void for being too remote. The school became the absolute owner, and the 'threat'
of the land returning was removed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Rule against Perpetuity (Section 14 TPA): Applies to 'rights of reverter' and future contingent interests.
2. Conditions that might trigger a transfer after the perpetuity period are void.
3. This ensures that land is not burdened with 'shadow interests' for centuries.

cases.title: Abdul Khader v. Hussein Saheb
cases.facts:
A person needed Rs. 5,000. He 'sold' his house to a lender for that amount and registered the sale deed. On the
same day, but in a separate document, the lender signed an agreement promising to sell the house back to
the borrower if he paid Rs. 5,000 within 5 years. The borrower didn't pay in 5 years but later sued to 'redeem'
the house, claiming it was a mortgage.
cases.issues:
1. Can two separate documents (a Sale and an Agreement to Repurchase) be read together to create a
'Mortgage by Conditional Sale'?
2. What is the effect of the Proviso to Section 58(c) of the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The borrower argued that the 'intent' was a loan. The two documents were signed on the same day at the same
time. Therefore, they should be treated as one mortgage transaction.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that under the strict proviso added to Section 58(c) in 1929, a transaction cannot be a
mortgage unless the condition of repurchase is written in the same document as the sale. Since they were
separate papers, it was an absolute sale.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the lender, holding it was an absolute 'Sale'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive interpretation of the Proviso to Section 58(c). The legislature added this
proviso specifically to end the massive litigation over whether a sale was a mortgage. The law now says: 'No
such transaction shall be deemed to be a mortgage unless the condition is embodied in the document which
effects or purports to effect the sale.' The Court held that even if the intent was a mortgage, the failure to put the
condition in the same document is a fatal statutory error. The two-document transaction is legally a 'Sale
with a separate option to repurchase'. Since the option was not exercised in 5 years, the borrower lost all rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 58(c) Proviso: Same document rule is mandatory for a 'Mortgage by Conditional Sale'.
2. Two separate documents can never create a mortgage, regardless of the parties' intent.
3. Registration of two separate deeds results in a Sale and an Option, not a security.

cases.title: Vikas Sales Corp v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes
cases.facts:
The case involved the transfer of Export-Import (EXIM) scrips. The question before the Supreme Court was
whether these scrips were 'actionable claims' or 'goods'. If they were actionable claims, they would be exempt
from Sales Tax, as the definition of 'goods' in the Sale of Goods Act and various Sales Tax Acts excludes
actionable claims.
cases.issues:
1. What is the precise definition of an 'Actionable Claim' under Section 3 of the TPA?
2. Are tradable entitlements like EXIM scrips mere debts or independent movable property?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The traders argued that scrips represent a right to receive a license or a debt from the government. It is a claim
to a beneficial interest not in possession, fitting the TPA definition of an actionable claim.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The State argued that scrips are freely bought and sold in the market like commodities. They are 'incorporeal'
movable property, having a value in themselves, and thus should be treated as goods.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that EXIM scrips are 'goods' and not 'actionable claims'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that an actionable claim is a debt that can be enforced only through legal action. EXIM scrips,
however, are instruments that represent a crystallized right to import, which can be transferred by mere
delivery. They are 'property' that can be enjoyed by the holder without the need for a lawsuit. Since they have
an independent market value and are tradable, they are classified as incorporeal movable property. The TPA's
definition of actionable claims is intended to cover unsecured debts and similar claims, not marketable
commercial rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Actionable Claims (Sec 3 TPA) are limited to unsecured debts and beneficial interests in movable
property not in possession.
2. Marketable intangible rights (like scrips, patents, trademarks) are 'goods'.
3. The power to transfer the right by delivery indicates the item is property and not a mere claim.

cases.title: Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal
cases.facts:
During the hearing of an election petition, the defendant and his counsel failed to appear on a specific day. The
Tribunal proceeded ex-parte. Later, the defendant appeared and requested the court to 'set aside' the ex-parte
proceedings and allow him to take part. The Tribunal refused, arguing that procedural laws regarding non-
appearance must be strictly applied.
cases.issues:
1. Does a court have the inherent power to undo a procedural hardship caused by non-appearance?
2. What is the 'right to be heard' in the context of property and civil disputes?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The appellant argued that procedural law is the 'handmaid' of justice. A technical default should not result in a
person losing their rights without a fair trial.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The respondent argued that the rules of procedure are mandatory. Once a party is negligent, the court cannot
keep turning back the clock.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the defendant, emphasizing the flexibility of procedural law.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that our laws of procedure are based on the principle that 'no man shall be condemned unheard'.
A code of procedure is designed to facilitate justice and further its ends; it is a handmaid and not a mistress. If a
party can show 'sufficient cause' for their absence, the court must lean toward allowing them to participate. The
Court noted that in matters involving substantive rights, procedural technicalities should not be used as traps
for litigants.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Procedural law is a handmaid of justice, not its master.
2. The principle of audi alteram partem is the bedrock of judicial and quasi-judicial proceedings.
3. Courts possess inherent powers to ensure fairness over technicality.

cases.title: Rajender Singh v. Santa Singh
cases.facts:
A person was in 'Adverse Possession' of a property. During the 12-year period required to perfect his title, the
real owner filed a lawsuit for possession. However, the lawsuit was dismissed on a technicality. After the 12
years were up, the owner filed a second suit. The occupant argued that the first suit did not 'interrupt' his
possession and that the doctrine of 'Lis Pendens' prevented the owner from stopping the clock.
cases.issues:
1. Does the filing of a suit for possession interrupt the period of 'Adverse Possession'?
2. Does 'Lis Pendens' apply to a person who is claiming title through adverse possession?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued that by filing the suit, he had actively challenged the occupant's claim. Therefore, the
possession was no longer 'peaceful' or 'unchallenged'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The occupant argued that since the first suit failed, it was as if it never happened. Lis Pendens only protects
transfers by 'act of parties', not title gained through the law of limitation.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the suit did interrupt the adverse possession.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that adverse possession must be 'peaceful and continuous'. The moment the real owner files a
suit to evict the trespasser, the 'peace' of the possession is broken. Even if the suit is delayed or dismissed on a
technicality, the intent to reclaim the land has been legally manifested. The Court also clarified that the doctrine
of Lis Pendens (Section 52 TPA) is designed to protect the res (the property) from being alienated by the
parties, and it ensures that the owner's legal battle is not frustrated by time-barring while the case is in court.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Adverse possession is interrupted by the institution of a suit for possession by the true owner.
2. Possession must be 'hostile' and 'peaceful' to ripen into title.
3. Lis Pendens serves the public policy of ensuring litigation reaches a meaningful conclusion.

cases.title: Gopalakrishna v. Narayan
cases.facts:
A property was settled on a person (A) with a condition that if (A) died without male issue, the property should
go to (B). (A) died without having any children. However, before (A) died, (B) had already died. The heirs of
(B) claimed the property, while the heirs of (A) argued that since (B) died first, he never got the property.
cases.issues:
1. When does a 'Contingent Interest' become a 'Vested Interest'?
2. Does the death of a remainderman before the contingency happens defeat the interest of his heirs?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs of (B) argued that the moment the condition (death of A without issue) was met, the right 'vested' in
B's estate. The fact that B was dead is irrelevant, as he possessed a 'transmissible' interest.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The heirs of (A) argued that (B) had to be alive to take the gift. A dead person cannot acquire property.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of (B)'s heirs.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that according to Section 21 of the TPA, a contingent interest depends on an uncertain event.
However, unlike a personal right, a contingent interest in property is 'heritable' and 'transferable' (unless the
contract says otherwise). Since the event (A dying childless) actually happened, the property must flow to B's
heirs. The right of B was not 'personal' to him but was a right in the property that his heirs inherited.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Contingent interests are generally transmissible to heirs.
2. Once the contingency is fulfilled, the interest vests automatically in the transferee or their estate.
3. Property law favors the vesting of interests rather than their lapse.

cases.title: R. Hemalatha v. Kasthuri
cases.facts:
This recent case dealt with an unregistered 'Agreement to Sell' that contained a clause regarding the delivery of
possession. Under the 2001 amendment to the Registration Act, such agreements must be registered to be used
as evidence in a suit for 'Specific Performance'. The plaintiff sought to enforce the agreement even though it
was unregistered, relying on a state-specific amendment in Tamil Nadu.
cases.issues:
1. Can an unregistered Agreement to Sell be admitted as evidence in a suit for specific performance?
2. What is the effect of Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act on the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The plaintiff argued that Section 49 of the Registration Act provides a 'proviso' allowing unregistered
documents to be used as evidence for 'collateral transactions' and specifically for suits of specific performance.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The defendant argued that the 2001 amendment made registration mandatory for agreements involving
possession (Section 17(1A)). If the document isn't registered, it is legally 'non-existent' for the court.
cases.judgment:
Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the unregistered agreement was admissible for the limited purpose of a
suit for specific performance.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified the interplay between Section 17 and Section 49 of the Registration Act. While Section
17(1A) mandates registration for agreements to sell involving possession to claim the benefit of 'Part
Performance' (Section 53A TPA), it does not take away the right to sue for 'Specific Performance'. The Court
held that the proviso to Section 49 specifically allows an unregistered document to be received as evidence of a
contract in a suit for specific performance. Thus, the plaintiff can still ask the court to force the seller to execute
a registered deed.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Unregistered Agreements to Sell are admissible in suits for Specific Performance (Section 49 Proviso,
Registration Act).
2. Registration is mandatory to claim the shield of 'Part Performance' under Sec 53A TPA.
3. The lack of registration does not bar the substantive right to enforce a contract.

cases.title: B.R. Koteswara Rao v. G. Rameshwara Bai
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his property. The mortgage deed had a clause that the lender could 'enjoy the profits' of the
land for 99 years and that no interest would be charged, but the property could not be redeemed before the 99-
year term ended. The owner's grandson sued to redeem the property early, claiming the 99-year term was a
'clog'.
cases.issues:
1. Does a very long period of mortgage (99 years) always constitute a 'Clog on Redemption'?
2. How do courts assess 'unconscionability' in mortgages?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The grandson argued that 99 years meant the family would never practically get the land back. It was a device
to transform a mortgage into a permanent lease or ownership, which equity prohibits.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that the terms were beneficial: the borrower got a large sum and paid 'zero' interest for a
century. It was a fair commercial deal for agricultural development.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled that the 99-year term was a 'clog' and allowed early redemption.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that while the length of time (99 years) is not per se a clog, it must be looked at in the context
of the parties' circumstances. If the period is so long that it practically makes the right to redeem 'illusory' or
'meaningless' for the owner and his immediate heirs, and if the lender is getting a disproportionate benefit (like
keeping all profits without accounting), it is a clog. The Court held that the purpose of a mortgage is only to
secure a debt, and the lender cannot use it to 'grab' the property for a century. The owner was allowed to pay the
debt and take the land back.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. A long postponement of redemption is a clog if it makes the right to redeem illusory.
2. Courts will look behind the 'form' of the deed to the 'substance' of the fairness.
3. 'Equity of Redemption' is a protected right that cannot be bargained away through oppressive terms.

cases.title: Champa Ram v. Kunwar Singh
cases.facts:
A mortgagor (borrower) failed to pay the debt. The mortgagee (lender) took possession of the land. The
borrower later died. His heirs didn't sue for redemption for 50 years. The lender's heirs then argued they had
become the absolute owners by 'adverse possession' and that the mortgage had 'merged' with their possession.
cases.issues:
1. Can a mortgagee in possession ever become the owner through the passage of time?
2. What is the effect of Section 60 TPA on stale mortgage claims?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The lender's heirs argued that 50 years of possession without any payment or interference from the owner
proved they were holding the land as owners. The owner's 'silence' for half a century was a waiver of his rights.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The borrower's heirs argued 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage'. Until the statutory period of 60 years
(under the old law) or 30 years (under the new law) passed, they had a right to redeem.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Privy Council ruled in favor of the borrower's heirs.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reaffirmed that as long as the relationship of 'mortgagor and mortgagee' exists, the possession of the
lender can never be 'adverse' to the borrower. The lender is in possession 'under the mortgage' and not in
defiance of it. To start a claim for adverse possession, the lender must first prove he 'renounced' the mortgage
and began holding the land as a hostile outsider to the owner's knowledge. Since no such act occurred, the
mortgage was still alive, and the borrower's heirs could redeem it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mortgagee's possession is permissive and cannot ripen into adverse possession.
2. The Right of Redemption survives until the last day of the limitation period (Section 60 TPA).
3. 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage'.

cases.title: Rajeshwar v. Dashrathlal
cases.facts:
A person owned a large piece of land. He sold the 'northern half' to (A) and the 'southern half' to (B). The only
well for water was located in the northern half. The sale deed to (B) did not mention any right to use the well.
(A) later blocked (B) from using the well. (B) sued, claiming a right of easement.
cases.issues:
1. What is an 'Easement by Implication of Law' under Section 8 of the TPA?
2. Does the sale of land include all 'quasi-easements' used by the previous owner?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The buyer of the southern half (B) argued that when the owner held the whole land, he used the well for both
parts. This was an 'apparent and continuous' use. When the land was split, the right to the water passed to him
as a 'legal incident' of the land.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The buyer of the northern half (A) argued that he bought the land 'with the well'. He paid for it, and since B's
deed was silent, B had no right to trespass on A's property to take water.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of (B), upholding the easement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that under Section 8 of the TPA, a transfer of property passes to the transferee all the
'easements' annexed to it. Furthermore, it applied the principle of 'Quasi-Easements'. If an owner of two plots
uses one to benefit the other in a visible and permanent way (like a well or a drain), and then sells the plots to
different people, the law presumes that the right continues for the benefit of the purchaser unless the deed
explicitly excludes it. Since the well was the only source of water and was visibly used for the whole land, B
acquired an implied easement to use it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 8 TPA: Transfers include all 'legal incidents' and annexed easements.
2. Quasi-Easements pass to the transferee by implication if they are apparent and continuous.
3. The law prevents a 'derogation from grant' (a seller cannot take away what is necessary to enjoy the
gift/sale).

cases.title: Tulsi v. Chandrika Prasad
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his house. The lender (mortgagee) was a very wealthy man, while the borrower was poor.
The mortgage deed was for 99 years. It also contained a clause that if the borrower failed to pay any single
annual interest installment, the lender could 'immediately' foreclose and become the absolute owner. The
borrower missed one installment due to illness, and the lender claimed the house.
cases.issues:
1. Can a 'single default' clause in a mortgage lead to the absolute loss of property?
2. What is the role of 'Equity' in protecting mortgagors from harsh 'forfeiture' clauses?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The borrower argued that the 99-year term and the 'single default' clause were designed to steal his house. It
was an unconscionable bargain and a clog on his right to redeem.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The lender argued that the borrower signed the deed with full knowledge. A contract is sacred, and the penalty
for default was clearly stated and agreed upon.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the borrower, striking down the forfeiture clause.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that the 'Right of Redemption' is a statutory heart of the TPA (Section 60) and is based on the
equitable principle that a lender should only get his money back, not the borrower's land. A 'single default'
leading to total loss of property is the most extreme form of a 'Clog on Redemption'. It is a penalty clause that
shocks the conscience of the court. The Court ruled that such clauses are void. The borrower was allowed to
pay the arrears and keep his house. The Court noted that in mortgages, the 'forfeiture' of the owner's interest is
always viewed with extreme disfavor.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Forfeiture clauses in mortgages are void as 'clogs'.
2. Equity protects vulnerable borrowers from 'unconscionable' terms.
3. The right to redeem cannot be lost through a mere procedural or minor financial default.

cases.title: Gopal Sridhar v. Shashi Bhushan
cases.facts:
A person took three different loans from the same bank at different times. For each loan, he mortgaged a
different piece of land (Plot A, Plot B, and Plot C). Later, he wanted to repay the loan for Plot A and take it
back. The bank refused, arguing that he must pay off all three loans together or he cannot redeem any of the
plots. This is the doctrine of 'Consolidation'.
cases.issues:
1. What is the 'Doctrine of Consolidation' of mortgages?
2. Does Section 61 of the TPA allow a mortgagor to redeem one mortgage without redeeming others?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The borrower argued that under Section 61, he had a right to redeem any one mortgage separately. The bank
was trying to 'consolidate' his debts against his will.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The bank argued that it was more secure to keep all three plots as a single pool of security for the total debt.
Releasing one plot would weaken their position.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the borrower, allowing the separate redemption.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified Section 61 of the TPA. In India, the 'Doctrine of Consolidation' was explicitly abolished by
the TPA unless there is a 'contract to the contrary'. The general rule is that a mortgagor who has executed two or
more mortgages in favor of the same mortgagee can redeem any one mortgage separately, or any two or more
of them together. The bank cannot force the borrower to pay all debts to save one piece of land. Since there was
no specific clause in the deeds allowing consolidation, the borrower had the right to free Plot A by paying only
the debt attached to it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 61 TPA: Mortgagor has the right to redeem mortgages separately (No Consolidation).
2. Consolidation is only allowed if there is an express contract between the parties.
3. Protects the borrower's flexibility in managing their property and debts.

cases.title: N. Ramaiah v. K.N. Narayana Reddy
cases.facts:
A property was owned by (A). He entered into an 'Agreement to Sell' with (B). While the agreement was still
active, (A) died. He left a 'Will' giving the property to his son (C). (B) sued for 'Specific Performance'. (C)
argued that the Will made him the new owner and that his father's personal contract with (B) did not bind him.
cases.issues:
1. Does an 'Agreement to Sell' create an interest in the property that binds the heirs of the seller?
2. What is the effect of Section 40 of the TPA on restrictive/affirmative covenants?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The buyer (B) argued that a contract to sell land is a 'covenant' that attaches to the property. Under Section 40, a
person who takes the property (like an heir or a donee) is bound by the prior obligations of the previous owner.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The son (C) argued that his father was the absolute owner and could change his mind by making a Will. A Will
is a later document and should prevail over a mere agreement.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the buyer (B).
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that under Section 40 of the TPA, an obligation arising out of a contract (like an agreement to
sell) can be enforced against a 'gratuitous transferee' (someone who gets property for free, like an heir or a
donee). The son, being an heir under a Will, did not pay for the property. Therefore, he 'stepped into the shoes'
of his father with all the father's 'burdens' intact. The contract to sell the land remained valid and the son was
legally bound to execute the sale deed in favor of (B) upon payment of the balance.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Section 40 TPA: Contractual obligations regarding land bind subsequent 'gratuitous' transferees (heirs,
donees).
2. Heirs of a seller are legally bound to honor an 'Agreement to Sell' made by the deceased.
3. Specific performance can be enforced against the estate of the deceased.

cases.title: Habiba Bibi v. Ram Sahai
cases.facts:
A person mortgaged his property and then went missing. His wife, who was in possession of the land, 'sold' the
property to a third party to pay off her own personal debts. When the husband (the real owner) eventually
returned, he sued to recover the property, arguing the sale by his wife was void because she was not the owner
and had no authority to sell.
cases.issues:
1. Can a person without title validly transfer property belonging to another?
2. What is the scope of Section 7 of the TPA regarding 'Competency' to transfer?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The husband argued Section 7 TPA: only an owner or an authorized agent can transfer property. The wife was
neither. The sale was a 'nullity'.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The purchaser argued that the wife appeared to be the owner in her husband's absence and that he bought it in
'good faith' to help the family.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the husband, declaring the sale void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly applied Section 7. A transfer of property is only valid if the transferor is 'competent to
contract' and 'entitled to transferable property', OR 'authorized to dispose of' property not his own. The wife
was not the owner, and her status as a wife did not give her an automatic 'authority' to sell her husband's land,
especially for her personal debts. Unlike 'legal necessity' in Hindu law for a widow, a wife during her husband's
lifetime cannot alienate his assets. The purchaser took the risk of buying from a person without title and must
suffer the loss.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Competency to Transfer (Section 7 TPA) is a mandatory prerequisite for a valid transfer.
2. A person cannot transfer a better title than they themselves possess (Nemo dat quod non habet).
3. Good faith of the purchaser cannot validate a sale by a person with zero legal authority.

cases.title: Raj Kumar v. Gopi Nath
cases.facts:
A landlord and tenant entered into a lease for a factory. The deed stated that the lease was 'for as long as the
tenant continues to pay the rent'. The landlord later tried to evict the tenant, arguing that a lease without a fixed
'end date' is a month-to-month tenancy that can be terminated at any time by giving a notice to quit.
cases.issues:
1. What is the legal status of a lease with an 'indefinite' duration?
2. Does Section 106 of the TPA apply to leases that purport to be 'permanent' but are not registered?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The landlord argued that under Section 106, a manufacturing lease without a written and registered fixed term
is legally deemed to be from 'year to year'. Since the deed was not registered, it was only a month-to-month
arrangement.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The tenant argued that the words 'as long as I pay' created a 'Permanent Lease' that could never be ended as
long as he was honest with the rent.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the landlord, holding it was a month-to-month lease.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that in Indian law, a 'Permanent Lease' (Section 107) must be made by a registered
instrument. An unregistered deed or an oral agreement can never create a permanent interest. Under Section
106, if there is no valid registered contract to the contrary, the law 'deems' the lease to be based on the purpose:
for manufacturing, it is year-to-year; for others, month-to-month. The phrase 'as long as I pay' is too vague to
override the statutory presumption. The landlord's notice to quit was valid.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Permanent Leases must be registered (Section 107 TPA).
2. Section 106 TPA creates legal 'presumptions' for the duration of leases in the absence of a registered
contract.
3. Indefinite language in an unregistered deed results in a terminable tenancy.

cases.title: Ramrao v. Laxman
cases.facts:
A donor gifted his property to his two sons, (A) and (B), with the condition that 'the property shall be divided
between you only after you both reach the age of 21'. Son (A) died at the age of 19. His widow claimed his
half-share. Son (B) argued that since (A) never reached 21, he never 'got' the property and his interest was
gone.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'postponement of enjoyment' create a contingent interest or a vested interest?
2. What is the effect of an age-condition under Section 19 and 21 of the TPA?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The widow argued that the gift was absolute. The 'age of 21' was only a limit on when they could 'partition' or
'use' the land, not on when they became the 'owners'. Therefore, it was a vested interest.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The brother argued that 'reaching 21' was a 'Condition Precedent'. Since the brother didn't fulfill the condition,
the gift to him failed.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the widow, holding the interest was 'Vested'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 19 of the TPA. It held that an interest is 'vested' when it is not subject to a condition
precedent. A condition that merely 'postpones' the time of enjoyment (like reaching a certain age) does not
make the interest contingent. The moment the deed was signed, the sons became the owners. The 'age 21' rule
was only about managing the land. Since the ownership had already passed to (A), it was part of his estate
when he died, and his widow inherited it. The law favors 'early vesting' of property.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Postponement of possession or enjoyment does not make an interest contingent (Section 19 TPA).
2. A gift to a person 'upon reaching a certain age' is generally treated as a vested interest unless the
language is clearly conditional.
3. Vested interests are heritable regardless of whether the transferee was in possession.

cases.title: Shri Ram Mandir v. State
cases.facts:
A donor gifted land to a charitable hospital. The deed contained a clause: 'The hospital shall use the land only
for a maternity ward and shall never, under any circumstances, sell, lease, or mortgage any part of this land to
anyone'. Years later, the hospital needed to lease a small corner to a chemist shop to raise funds for medicines.
The donor's family sued to stop the lease, citing the 'no-alienation' clause.
cases.issues:
1. Is a condition 'absolutely' restraining the alienation of property given for charity valid?
2. Does Section 10 of the TPA apply to 'Public Trusts' or charities?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The heirs argued that the hospital accepted the land for a specific purpose. They must honor the 'no-sale' rule as
a matter of religious and moral duty.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The hospital argued that a total ban on alienation is void under Section 10. They needed to lease a part to fulfill
the 'main' purpose of the gift (healing people).
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the hospital, holding the restriction on alienation was void.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied Section 10 of the TPA. It held that the rule against 'Absolute Restraint on Alienation' is a rule
of public policy that applies to all transfers of property. Once you transfer the 'ownership' of property, you
cannot take away the 'power' to alienate it. A condition that says 'you can never sell or lease' is an absolute
restraint and is void in law. The hospital was the owner and had the right to manage its assets, including leasing
them for its charitable objectives. The 'shadow' of the donor's control cannot last forever.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Absolute restraints on alienation are void (Section 10 TPA).
2. This rule applies even to charitable or religious transfers.
3. Ownership and the power of alienation are inseparable in property law.

cases.title: Laxman v. Bayabai
cases.facts:
A person made a will giving his house to his wife. The will stated: 'My wife shall be the owner, but if she fails
to live in this house and moves back to her parents' city, her ownership shall cease and the house shall go to my
brother'. The wife moved back to her parents' city after two years. The brother sued for possession.
cases.issues:
1. Is a condition requiring 'residence' a valid 'Condition Subsequent' (Section 31)?
2. Can a property right be made to end if a person changes their place of living?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The brother argued that the husband had a right to ensure his wife stayed in the family home. The 'failure to
reside' was a specific event that triggered the end of her interest under Section 31.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The wife argued that such a condition was a restraint on her personal liberty and 'unreasonable', and therefore
void under Section 25.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the brother, upholding the condition.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Section 31 of the TPA allows for 'Determinable Interests'. A donor can set a condition that
an interest shall 'cease to exist' upon the happening of a certain event. The condition to 'live in the house' is not
illegal, immoral, or impossible. It was a valid choice given to the wife. Since she chose to leave, the condition
subsequent was fulfilled, her title was extinguished by operation of law, and the property moved to the brother.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Conditions Subsequent (Section 31 TPA) can legally terminate an existing interest.
2. Conditions regarding residence or personal conduct are valid unless they are 'immoral' or 'illegal'.
3. The property 'shifts' automatically upon the breach of the condition.

cases.title: Ram Baran v. Ram Iqbal
cases.facts:
Two neighbors, (A) and (B), signed an agreement: 'If (A) ever builds a second story on his house, he must pay
(B) Rs. 10,000 because it will block (B)'s sunlight'. Years later, (A) sold his house to (C). (C) built a second
story. (B) sued (C) for the Rs. 10,000. (C) argued he never signed the agreement.
cases.issues:
1. Does a 'Personal Covenant' (a promise to pay money) bind a subsequent purchaser of the land?
2. What is the difference between a 'Covenant Running with the Land' (Section 40) and a 'Personal
Contract'?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The neighbor (B) argued that the promise was 'annexed' to the land. Since (C) bought the house with 'notice' of
the agreement, he must honor the debt attached to the use of the land.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The new owner (C) argued that he bought the 'land', not the 'debts' of the previous owner. A promise to pay
money is a personal matter (right in personam) and doesn't 'stick' to the property.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled in favor of (C), holding the covenant did not bind him.
cases.reasoning:
The Court clarified Section 40 of the TPA. Covenants that 'run with the land' are usually 'restrictive' (promises
not to do something). An 'affirmative' covenant (a promise to pay money or do an act) is generally
considered a 'personal' obligation. Under Indian law, you cannot attach a 'money burden' to a piece of land that
binds all future owners, as it would make property transfers too complex. Since (C) was not a party to the
contract, he was not liable for (A)'s promise. (B) could only sue (A) for breach of contract.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Affirmative covenants (to pay money) do not run with the land and do not bind transferees.
2. Section 40 TPA primarily protects 'restrictive' (negative) covenants against purchasers with notice.
3. Property law protects the freedom of purchasers from unknown personal debts of the seller.

cases.title: M.P. Housing Board v. Krishna Kumari
cases.facts:
A government housing board allowed a person to occupy a stall in a market. The document said the occupant
was a 'licensee' and that the board could 'evict him at any time' without notice. The occupant, however, put up a
permanent shutter, kept the keys, and paid a fixed 'rent'. The board later tried to evict him summarily. He
claimed he was a 'tenant'.
cases.issues:
1. Can the government bypass rent laws by labeling every allotment as a 'License'?
2. Is the power to 'evict at any time' compatible with a lease?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The occupant argued that he had 'Exclusive Possession'. He could lock the stall and go home. This control
makes him a lessee under Section 105 TPA.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The Board argued that as a public body, they only granted a 'permission' to use the stall for public convenience.
The reservation of the right to evict at any time proves they never intended to part with the 'interest' in the land.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Supreme Court ruled it was a 'License'.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that in 'Government Allotments', the 'Public Purpose' is the dominant factor. Unlike private
deals, the government often retains 'overriding control' for public safety and town planning. The Court found
that the Housing Board had the right to enter and inspect the stalls at any time and that the stall was part of a
larger public market complex. Because the Board did not truly grant 'Exclusive Possession' in the proprietary
sense, and the right to evict at any time was a key term, the arrangement was a License. The occupant had no
permanent rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Government allotments for specific public purposes are often construed as Licenses.
2. 'Overriding Control' by the owner prevents the creation of a Lease.
3. The 'Public Interest' can influence the interpretation of the parties' intent.

cases.title: Kunda v. Onkar
cases.facts:
A person entered into an oral agreement to sell his land. He took the full price and handed over physical
possession to the buyer. However, he refused to sign a registered sale deed. When the buyer sued to stay in
possession, the seller argued that under Section 54, an oral sale of land over Rs. 100 is 'zero' in law. The buyer
claimed 'Part Performance' under Section 53A.
cases.issues:
1. Can the doctrine of 'Part Performance' (Section 53A) be based on an 'Oral' agreement?
2. What are the mandatory requirements for 53A protection?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The buyer argued that he had paid the money and was living on the land. Equity should protect him from being
cheated by the seller.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The seller argued that Section 53A explicitly says the contract must be 'in writing signed by him'. An oral
promise is not a contract in property law.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the seller, rejecting the 53A claim.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that Section 53A of the TPA is a statutory rule and must be followed strictly. It requires (1) a
contract 'in writing', (2) 'signed' by the transferor, and (3) terms that are 'ascertainable with reasonable
certainty'. The Court ruled that 'Equity' cannot override the clear words of the TPA. Since there was no written
and signed paper, the buyer had no defense against eviction. He could only sue to get his money back, but he
could not keep the land. This case highlights the vital importance of 'writing' in real estate.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Doctrine of Part Performance (Section 53A TPA) requires a 'Written and Signed' contract.
2. Oral agreements for sale of immovable property afford no protection against eviction.
3. TPA formalities are mandatory and exclude general equitable 'fairness' claims.

cases.title: Noakes & Co. v. Rice
cases.facts:
A man mortgaged his farm. The lender was his neighbor. The neighbor said: 'I will lend you the money, but
even after you pay me back, you must allow me to use the shortcut path across your farm forever'. The man
paid the debt and then blocked the neighbor, saying the 'path-right' ended with the mortgage.
cases.issues:
1. Can a mortgagee acquire a permanent 'Easement' or right as a condition of a loan?
2. Does such a right survive the redemption of the mortgage?
cases.arguments:
A. Plaintiff / Appellant
The owner argued 'Once a mortgage, always a mortgage'. The property must return to him in its 'original' state.
An easement is a permanent burden that devalues his farm.
B. Defendant / Respondent
The neighbor argued that it was a separate gift or agreement made at the time of the loan. He claimed it was a
'collateral' benefit that was fair.
cases.judgment: Ruling: The Court ruled in favor of the owner, striking down the easement.
cases.reasoning:
The Court held that a mortgagee cannot use his position of power (the lender) to extract a benefit that lasts
longer than the mortgage itself. This is a 'clog' because it prevents the owner from getting his property back
'unfettered'. Redemption means the 'complete' restoration of the property. Any 'string' attached to the property
that survives the payment of the debt is void. The farm had to be returned free of the neighbor's claim.
cases.legalPrinciples:
1. Mortgagee cannot gain any benefit that outlives the mortgage debt.
2. Collateral benefits that permanently burden the land are 'clogs' and are void.
3. The status quo of the property must be restored upon redemption.
